profileDesc.creation:
Initially created: 2025-12-06T12:07:19.357+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.
Input text:

p.seg: I, your servant, [Sòng] Cháo Sàn Dà Fū Yòu Jiàn Yì Dà Fū Quán Yù Shǐ Zhōng Chéng Chōng Lǐ Jiǎn Shǐ Shàng Hù Jūn Cì Zǐ Jīn Yú Dài,
have been commanded to compile [this work].
Hòu Xué Tiān Tái
The Ěryǎ states: When the Grand Year Star is in the [position of] Jiǎ, it is called Èfēng.
When in Yǐ, it is called Zhānméng.
When in Bǐng, it is called Ròuzhào.
When in Dīng, it is called Qiángyǔ.
When in Wù, it is called Zhùyōng.
When in Jǐ, it is called Túwéi.
When in Gēng, it is called Shàngzhāng.
When in Xīn, it is called Chóngguāng.
When in Rén, it is called Xuányì.
When in Guǐ, it is called Zhāoyáng.
These are the Year Stems (Suìyáng).
When in Yín, it is called Shèdīgé.
When in Mǎo, it is called Dān'è.
When in Chén, it is called Zhíxú.
When in Sì, it is called Dàhuāngluò.
When in Wǔ, it is called Dūnzāng.
When in Wèi, it is called Xiéxiá.
When in Shēn, it is called Tūntān.
When in Yǒu, it is called Zuò'è.
When in Xū, it is called Yǎnmào.
When in Hài, it is called Dàyuānxiàn.
When in Zǐ, it is called Kùndūn.
When in Chǒu, it is called Chìfènruò.
These are the Year Branches (Suìmíng).
The annotation to the Zhōu Jì says:
"Starting from Zhùyōng Shèdīgé"
means starting from Wùyín.
"Ending at Xuányì Kùndūn"
means ending at Rénzǐ.
È
is read as written;
the Shǐjì writes it as
"yān",
pronounced `yú gān' fān.
Zhù,
pronounced `chén rú' fān.
Yōng,
pronounced `yú róng' fān.
Yì,
pronounced `yì zhí' fān.
Dān'è,
the first character is pronounced dān,
also `tè lián' fān;
the second is pronounced `wū gé' fān,
also `yú lián' fān.
Zāng,
pronounced `zuò láng' fān.
Tūn,
pronounced `tǔ hún' fān.
Tān,
pronounced `tǔ dān' fān.
Kùndūn,
pronounced dùn.
Dù Yù's Shìzú Pǔ says: The Zhōu [dynasty]
were descendants of the Huángdì,
with the surname Jī.
Descendants of Hòujì,
they were enfeoffed in Tái.
When the Xià [dynasty] declined,
Jì's son Bùzhú fled to the Xīróng.
By the twelfth generation, his descendant Tàiwáng
fled from the Dí and moved to Qí.
By his grandson Wénwáng, who received the Mandate,
Wǔwáng conquered Shāng and possessed the world.
From Wǔwáng to Píngwáng, there were thirteen generations.
From Píngwáng to Wēilièwáng, there were another eighteen generations.
From Wēilièwáng to Nǎnwáng, there were another five generations.
Zhāng Shǒujié says: Because Tàiwáng resided in Zhōuyuán,
the state was named Zhōu.
The Dìlǐ Zhì says: In Měiyáng county, Qífēng mountain, northwest of Zhōuyuán in Zhōngshuǐxiang, Yòufúfēng,
was the capital of Zhōu Tàiwáng.
The Kuòdì Zhì says: The old Zhōu city, also known as Měiyáng city,
is twenty-five lǐ northwest of Wǔgōng county, Yōngzhōu.
Jì
means order,
to systematically order all affairs and link them to years and months.
Wēn Gōng used the method of the Chūnqiū for dating,
and, following the imperial annals (Běnjì) of the Shǐ and Hàn [histories], called them Jì.
Tái,
pronounced `tāng lái' fān.
Xià,
pronounced `hù yǎ' fān.
Zhú,
pronounced `zhú lǜ' fān.
Zai Yong,
pronounced `yú yòng' fān.
Wēilièwáng
was named Wǔ,
the son of Kǎowáng.
The rules for posthumous titles say: Fierce and resolute is called Wēi;
having achievements and bringing peace to the people is called Liè.
Shěn Yuē says: For all compound posthumous titles,
there is a person to be given a posthumous title,
but no fixed rules for the title itself.
1 Initially, the Zhōu king commanded the Jin grandees Wèi Sī, Zhào Jí, and Hán Qián to become feudal lords.
This is where Wēn Gōng's method of writing history began.
The ancestors of Wèi,
descendants of Bì Gōng Gāo,
shared the same surname as Zhōu.
Their descendant, Bì Wàn,
was first enfeoffed in Wèi.
By Wèi Shū,
they first became the principal minister of Jìn;
three generations later came Sī.
The ancestors of Zhào,
descendants of Zàofù.
By Shúdài,
they first moved from Zhōu to Jìn.
By Zhào Sù,
they were first enfeoffed in Gěng.
By Zhào Dùn,
they first became the principal minister of Jìn;
six generations later came Jí.
The ancestors of Hán
were descended from Zhōu Wǔwáng.
By Hán Wǔzǐ, who served Jìn,
they were enfeoffed in Hányuán.
By Hán Jué,
they became the principal minister of Jìn;
six generations later came Qián.
These three families
had for generations been grandees of Jìn,
and with respect to the Zhōu, they were merely subordinate officials.
The Zhōu royal house had already declined,
and Jìn was the leader of the summer alliance,
in order to honor the royal house,
hence it was commanded to be the Hegemon.
The three ministers usurped the power of Jìn,
tyrannized and scorned their lord,
and divided his state.
This was something the royal law ought to have punished.
Wēilièwáng not only could not punish them,
but also appointed them as feudal lords.
This was to exalt and encourage treacherous officials who violated their proper station.
The Zīzhì Tōngjiàn begins here,
is it not precisely to emphasize the proper distinctions of name and status?
Your servant [Sīmǎ] Guāng says: Your servant has heard that among the duties of the Son of Heaven, none is greater than ritual (lǐ).
Among rituals, none is greater than distinction (fèn).
Among distinctions, none is greater than name (míng).
What is ritual?
It is the principles and norms.
What is distinction?
It is ruler and minister.
What is name?
It is Gōng, Hóu, Qīng, Dàfū.
With the vastness of the four seas,
and the multitude of people,
subject to the control of one person,
even those with extraordinary strength
and superior wisdom
all
hurry about to serve.
Is this not because ritual serves as the principles and norms
for them?
Therefore, the Son of Heaven leads the Three Dukes;
the Three Dukes command the feudal lords;
the feudal lords govern the Qīng and Dàfū;
the Qīng and Dàfū rule the scholars and common people.
The noble governs the humble,
and the humble serves the noble.
The superior employing the inferior is like the heart and belly moving the hands and feet,
or the root controlling the branches and leaves.
The inferior serving the superior is like the hands and feet protecting the heart and belly,
or the branches and leaves sheltering the roots.
Only then can superior and inferior protect each other, and the state achieve peace and order.
Therefore, it is said that among the duties of the Son of Heaven, none is greater than ritual.
Wénwáng ordered the Yìjīng,
taking Qián and Kūn as the beginning.
Kǒngzǐ commented on it, saying:
"Heaven is honored, earth is lowly;
Qián and Kūn are established.
The lowly and the exalted are arrayed,
the noble and the humble have their positions."
This means that the positions of ruler and minister are as unchangeable as heaven and earth.
The Chūnqiū criticizes the zhūhóu [feudal lords]
and honors the royal
house. Even if the king's men are insignificant,
they are ranked above the zhūhóu.
This shows that the sages never failed to be diligent in matters between ruler and minister.
If there is not the tyranny of Jié and Zhòu,
nor the benevolence of Tāng and Wǔ,
to whom the people flock,
and whom Heaven destines,
then the distinction between ruler and minister requires one to uphold loyalty and face death.
Therefore, if Wēizǐ were to replace Zhòu, then Chéngtāng would be accorded the honor of matching Heaven.
The Shǐjì states: Shāng Emperor Yì had three sons: the eldest was named Wēizǐ Qǐ,
the second was Zhōngyǎn,
and the youngest was Zhòu.
Zhòu's mother was the empress.
Emperor Yì wanted to establish Qǐ as the crown prince,
but the Grand Historian, citing the law, argued against it, saying:
"A son born of a wife
cannot be replaced by a son born of a concubine."
Thus, Zhòu was established.
Zhòu ultimately brought about the downfall of the Yīn dynasty through his tyranny.
Kǒng
[Zhèng]
likened the father to Heaven,
and paired him with it.
Of all great acts of filial piety,
none is greater than this.
This is what is meant by
"No honor for a father is greater than matching him with Heaven."
Furthermore, Master Kǒng said: The Lǐjì states that all things originate from Heaven,
and humans originate from their ancestors.
Since both are origins,
they can be paired.
Therefore, kings all pair their ancestors with Heaven.
The Shìfǎ [Rules for Posthumous Titles] states: To eliminate cruelty and remove tyranny is called Tāng.
However, the Shìfǎ originated in Zhōu;
it is likely that the Yīn people already had this title,
and the Zhōu people then adopted it as a posthumous title.
分 (fèn),
fú wèn fān.
長 (zhǎng),
zhī liǎng fān.
卒 (zú),
zǐ xù fān.
If Jìzhá were to rule Wú, then Tàibó would receive blood sacrifices.
King Shòumèng of Wú had four sons: the eldest was named Zhūfán,
the second Yúzhài,
the third Yúmò,
and the fourth Jìzhá.
Jìzhá was virtuous,
and Shòumèng wished to establish him,
but Jìzhá declined, refusing.
Therefore, Zhūfán was established.
When Zhūfán died,
he bequeathed the throne to Yúzhài,
intending for his brothers to succeed each other in order,
eventually to transmit the state to Jìzhá;
Jìzhá ultimately declined and fled.
Afterward, Guāng, son of Zhūfán, and Liáo, son of Yúmò, contended for the state,
leading to Fūchā,
and Wú subsequently perished.
Sacrificial animals are used in ancestral temple sacrifices,
hence "blood sacrifices."
Tàibó was
the founder of the state of Wú.
Fàn Níng said: Tài is
a term for great goodness;
bó is
the eldest.
He was the eldest son of King Tàidàn of Zhōu,
hence called Tàibó.
Lù Démíng said: Shòumèng,
mò gōng fān.
Yúzhài,
cè jiè fān.
Yúmò,
sound mò.
Indeed, the great principles of ritual cannot be disordered.
Therefore, it is said that no ritual is greater than distinctions.
Ritual [lǐ]
distinguishes between the noble and the humble,
orders the close and the distant,
regulates all things,
and governs all affairs.
Without titles, it cannot be manifested;
without implements, it cannot take form.
Titles name things,
implements differentiate them.
Only then can the upper and lower ranks clearly have their order.
This is the great principle of ritual.
If titles and implements are lost,
how can ritual alone survive?
In the past, Zhòngshū Yúxī had rendered meritorious service to Wèi.
He declined a city and requested a fányīng.
Kǒngzǐ considered it better to give him more cities.
Only titles and implements
cannot be lent to others;
they are what the gentleman manages.
If governance perishes, the state follows.
The Zuǒzhuàn states: Sūn Huánzǐ of Wèi led an army to battle the Qí army at Xīnzhù,
and the Wèi army was defeated.
Zhòngshū Yúxī of Xīnzhù rescued Sūn Huánzǐ,
and Huánzǐ thus escaped.
Afterward, the people of Wèi awarded him a city,
but he declined;
he requested a qǔxuán [curved chime stand] and fányīng to attend court,
which was granted.
Kǒngzǐ heard of it and said:
"It would have been better to give him more cities.
Only titles and implements cannot be lent to others."
Fányīng is
a horse ornament.
Fán refers to
an ornament on the horse's mane;
yīng refers to
an ornament on the horse's breast.
The Jìnzhì commentary states: The yīng on the horse's breast is like a rope for the lord's towel.
繁 (fán),
sound pú guān fān.
纓 (yīng),
yī yíng fān.
索 (suǒ),
xī gè fān.
Kǒngzǐ wished to rectify names first,
believing that if names were not rectified, the people would have no place to put their hands and feet.
See Lúnyǔ.
It was a small matter,
yet Kǒngzǐ regretted it;
rectifying names was
a minor task,
yet Kǒngzǐ prioritized it.
This is truly because if names and implements are disordered, the upper and lower ranks have no way to preserve each other.
Indeed, nothing originates from the subtle and accomplishes itself in the manifest.
The sage's foresight is far-reaching,
thus he can carefully attend to the subtle and govern it.
The common people's understanding is short-sighted,
thus they must wait until things become manifest before saving them.
Governing the subtle requires little effort but yields great success,
whereas saving the manifest exhausts effort yet cannot succeed.
The Yìjīng says:
"Walking on frost, hard ice arrives."
This is the line statement for Kūn, first six.
The Xiàng [Image] says:
"Walking on frost, hard ice:
the yin [force] begins to congeal.
Following its course,
it reaches hard ice."
"One day, two days, ten thousand subtle matters,"
these are words from Gāoyáo Mó.
Kǒng Ānguó commented: Jī is
subtle.
It means one should be vigilant about the subtleties of ten thousand affairs.
幾 (jī),
jū yī fān.
Therefore, it is said that no distinction is greater than names.
Alas!
Yōu and Lì lost their virtue,
the Way of Zhōu declined day by day,
the cosmic order and discipline scattered and broke,
the lower encroached upon the upper, and the upper was replaced.
The feudal lords arrogated military power to themselves,
referring to the likes of Duke Huán of Qí, Duke Wén of Jìn, up to Duke Dào, as well as King Zhuāng of Chǔ, Fūchāi of Wú.
Then
there were the six ministers of Jìn, the three families of Lǔ, and the Tián clan of Qí.
Yet the sacrifices to Wén and Wǔ still continued,
probably because the descendants of Zhōu were still able to maintain their proper status and title.
Why do I say this?
In the past, Duke Wén of Jìn had rendered great service to the royal house.
He requested the right to a "suì" from King Xiāng,
but King Xiāng refused,
saying:
"This is a royal prerogative.
There has never been a replacement of virtue with two kings,
which your uncle would also detest.
Otherwise,
if uncle had the land and the 'suì',
why would he request it?"
Duke Wén was thereupon fearful and dared not disobey.
During the rebellion of Tàishū Dài,
King Xiāng fled to Fàn.
Duke Wén of Jìn led an army to restore the King,
and killed Tàishū Dài.
After having settled King Xiāng in Jiá,
the King rewarded him with land,
which he declined;
he requested a "suì",
which the King refused, and so on.
Dù Yù said: "Suì" means cutting through the ground to make a path,
this was a burial rite for kings.
Feudal lords all lowered their coffins by suspending them.
"Wángzhāng" means
to make obvious the distinction between the king and the feudal lords.
In ancient times, the Son of Heaven referred to feudal lords of the same surname as "bófù" (paternal uncle older than father) or "shúfù" (paternal uncle younger than father).
Suì,
pronounced suì.
È,
pronounced wū lù fān.
Nán,
pronounced nǎi dàn fān.
Fàn,
pronounced fàn.
Láo,
pronounced lì dào fān.
Quē,
pronounced qí yuè fān.
Xuán,
pronounced xuán.
Jiù,
pronounced qí jiǔ fān.
Although the people of Zhōu were no more numerous than those of Zhū and Jǔ,
Cáo, Téng, Zhū, Jǔ
were small states in the Spring and Autumn period.
Jǔ,
pronounced jū xǔ fān.
and was the sovereign over All Under Heaven,
even the mighty Jìn, Chǔ, Qí, and Qín dared not oppress it,
why?
Solely because the proper status and title still existed.
As for the Jì clan in Lǔ,
Tián Cháng in Qí,
Bái Gōng in Chǔ,
Zhì Bó in Jìn,
Jìshì, a grandee of Lǔ,
since Jì Yǒu,
had generations in control of the government of Lǔ.
Jì Píngzǐ exiled Duke Zhāo,
Jì Kāngzǐ exiled Duke Āi,
yet they bowed to the north their whole lives,
not daring to usurp the state.
Tián Cháng,
is Chén Héng.
The Tián clan was originally the Chén clan;
Wēn Gōng avoided the national taboo.
The character
"Héng"
was changed
to "Cháng".
Chén Chéngzǐ obtained control of the state of Qí,
killed Kàn Zhǐ,
and assassinated Duke Jiǎn,
yet he also dared not establish himself.
The "Shǐjì Shìjiā" refers to Chén Jìngzhòng Wán as Tián Jìngzhòng Wán,
and Chén Chéngzǐ Héng as Tián Cháng,
hence the "Tōngjiàn" uses this as its basis.
Bái Gōng Shèng killed Zǐ Xī, the Ling Yin of Chǔ, and Zǐ Qī, the Sīmǎ.
Shí Qǐ said:
"Burn the treasury and assassinate the king!
Otherwise, it won't succeed!"
Bái Gōng said:
"Assassinating the king is inauspicious,
burning the treasury means no accumulation."
Zhì Bó, during the decline of Jìn,
controlled its state government,
and invaded neighboring states,
being the strongest among the grandees of Jìn;
he attacked Duke Chū of Jìn,
and Duke Chū died on the road.
Zhì Bó wanted to annex Jìn but dared not,
so he enthroned Duke Āi and elevated him.
However, he ultimately dared not,
was it because his strength was insufficient or his heart was not firm?
Rather, he feared violating proper names and infringing upon their proper status, thereby incurring universal condemnation.
Now the grandees of Jìn oppressed and slighted their lord,
divided the state of Jìn.
The "Shǐjì Liùguó Niánbiǎo" records: In the sixteenth year of King Dìng,
Zhào, Wèi, Hán destroyed Zhì Bó,
and consequently divided the state of Jìn into three.
Furthermore, they were granted honors and ranks,
making them join the ranks of feudal lords.
This means that the meager proper status and title could no longer be maintained and were utterly abandoned.
The rites of the former kings ended here!
Some people thought that at that time,
the Zhōu royal house was weak,
and the Three Jìn states were strong.
The three families divided the state of Jìn,
and it was then called
"the Three Jìn",
just like the later Three Qín and Three Qí.
Could this have been possible?
This is absolutely not the case.
Although the Three Jìn were strong,
if they had disregarded the condemnation of All Under Heaven and violated righteousness and encroached upon rites,
then they would have established themselves without asking the Son of Heaven.
If they had established themselves without asking the Son of Heaven,
they would have been rebellious ministers,
and if there were a lord like Huán or Wén in All Under Heaven,
he would surely have upheld rites and righteousness and campaigned against them.
Now they requested from the Son of Heaven and the Son of Heaven permitted it,
this means they received the mandate of the Son of Heaven to become feudal lords,
who then could punish them?
Therefore, the inclusion of the Three Jìn among the feudal lords
was not the Three Jìn destroying the rites,
but the Son of Heaven destroying them himself.
Alas!
Once the rites between lord and minister were destroyed,
then All Under Heaven competed for supremacy with intelligence and strength,
and this led to the descendants of sages and worthies, who were feudal lords,
having their altars of soil and grain utterly extinguished.
This refers to Qí and Sòng perishing at the hands of the Tián clan,
Lǔ, Chén, and Yuè perishing at the hands of Chǔ,
and Zhèng perishing at the hands of Hán.
Mǐn,
pronounced mí rěn fān,
means to exhaust,
also pronounced mí lín fān.
Máo Huǎng said: to sink,
to extinguish.
Is this not lamentable?
2 Initially,
Zhì Xuānzǐ intended to make Yáo his successor.
Zhì Guǒ said:
"He is not as good as Xiāo.
Wéi Zhāo says: Zhì Xuānzǐ
was Shēn, the son of Jìn minister Xún Lì.
Yáo
was Zhì Bó, son of Xuānzǐ,
posthumously named Xiāngzǐ.
Zhì Guǒ
was a member of the Zhì clan.
Xiāo
was Xuānzǐ's illegitimate son.
According to the method of posthumous names: 'Holy, good, and widely heard' is called Xuān.
This was an excessive compliment for the Zhì clan.
His lack of something was one (fault).
Wéi Zhāo says: 'Lack of benevolence.'
Many scribes of the Tōngjiàn commonly wrote
"beautiful beard,"
which is incorrect.
Guóyǔ writes
"beautiful sideburns,"
which we now follow.
【Zhāng: The twelve-line edition correctly writes
"bìn" (sideburns);
the Kǒng edition is the same.
The B yǐ eleven-line edition writes
"xū" (beard).
】 His skills and arts were fully sufficient, so he was worthy;
he was clever in writing and eloquent, so he was worthy;
Wéi Zhāo says: Jǐ (給),
'sufficient.'
Qiǎo wén (巧文),
'clever in literary composition.'
Jì (伎),
pronounced qú qǐ (渠綺) with changed tones.
Despite being like this, he was extremely unbenevolent.
If one relies on these five merits to overpower others, and acts with malevolence,
who can tolerate him?
Wéi Zhāo says: Dài (待),
'to depend on' or 'to allow.'
The Zhì clan will surely be destroyed."
(Zhì Xuānzǐ) did not listen.
Zhì Guǒ established a separate lineage with the Grand Historian
and became the Fǔ clan.
This event is recorded in the Guóyǔ.
According to Zuǒ Zhuàn, Duke Āi, twenty-third year,
Xún Yáo of Jìn attacked Qí,
which is the first mention of him in the commentary.
The twenty-third year of Āi
was the fifth year of Yuán Wáng in Shǐjì.
Xún Lì was
Zhì Wénzǐ.
In the fourteenth year of Dìng,
Zhì Wénzǐ was still mentioned in the commentary.
There is no record in the commentary of Zhì Xuānzǐ's affairs.
The discussion about establishing Yáo
must have taken place before the fifth year of Yuán Wáng.
Wéi Zhāo says: The Grand Historian (Tàishǐ) was in charge of clans and surnames,
a subordinate of the spring official in Zhōu Lǐ;
the Lesser Historian (Xiǎoshǐ) was in charge of establishing genealogies
and distinguishing generations (zhāo mù).
Zhèng Sīnóng's commentary says: The historical officials were primarily responsible for writing,
thus Hán Xuānzǐ, when visiting Lǔ,
observed the books at the Grand Historian's office.
Genealogies (Shìxì)
refer to works like Dìxì and Shìběn;
the Lesser Historian was in charge of establishing them.
Jiǎ Gōngyàn's commentary says: The commentary cites the Grand Historian to prove this,
because the Grand Historian was the chief of the historical officials,
and shared their duties.
It is likely that according to the Zhōu system,
the Lesser Historian established surnames and clans,
while the Grand Historian was in charge of their records.
Zhì Guǒ wished to avoid the disaster of the Zhì clan,
hence he established a separate lineage with the Grand Historian.
Sòng Qí's Guóyǔ Bǔyīn: Bié (別),
pronounced bìe (彼列);
also pronounced as written.
Among Zhào Jiǎnzǐ's sons,
the elder was named Bó Lǔ,
the younger was named Wú Xù.
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ was
Yāng, the grandson of Wénzǐ.
According to the method of posthumous names: 'Consistent in virtue without slackness' is called Jiǎn.
Bái Hǔ Tōng says: Zǐ (子),
'to multiply,'
continuously without end.
Zhào Qí says: Zǐ (子)
is a general term for a man.
Zhǎng (長),
pronounced zhǐ liǎng (知兩) with changed tones.
Unsure whom to establish (as successor),
(Zhào Jiǎnzǐ) then wrote words of instruction and admonition on two bamboo slips (jiǎn).

"Sages"
are those who possess both talent and virtue;
those who lack both are called "fools."
Those whose virtue surpasses their talent are called "gentlemen";
those whose talent surpasses their virtue are called "petty men."
In the art of selecting people, if one cannot obtain sages or gentlemen,
rather than obtaining petty men,
it is better to obtain fools.
Why is this?
Gentlemen use their talent to do good;
petty men use their talent to do evil.
Those who use their talent to do good,
their good reaches all limits;
those who use their talent to do evil,
their evil also reaches all limits.
Although a fool wishes to do evil,
his wisdom is not sufficient,
his strength is not overwhelming.
It is like a puppy attacking a person;
the person can control it.
A petty man's wisdom is sufficient to accomplish his treachery,
and his courage is sufficient to carry out his brutality.
This is a tiger with wings;
how can its harm not be great!
A tiger with added wings,
its harm is even greater.
*Yán*,
means reverence.
Those who are loved are easy to draw near;
those who are revered are easy to keep at a distance.
Therefore, those who scrutinize are often blinded by talent and neglect virtue.
From ancient times until now,
many ministers who brought chaos to the state,
and sons who ruined their families,
had talent in excess but lacked virtue,
leading to their downfall.
How could it be only Zhì Bó!
Therefore, if those who govern a state or manage a family can discern the distinction between talent and virtue and know the proper order of priority,
then what difficulty will there be in selecting people!

Sīmǎ (司馬)

Ráng (穰),

When Qǐ (起) was a general,

Qí (騎) means to ride a horse,
chéng (乘) means to ride a carriage,

means to carry on one’s back.
This means that Qǐ (起) personally carried the rations that the soldiers bore on their backs.
Yíng (贏),
pronounced yí chéng.
When a soldier had a carbuncle,

The soldier’s mother heard about this and wept.
Someone said:
“Your son
is a mere soldier, yet the general himself sucked his carbuncle,
why do you weep?”
The mother said:
“It is not so.
Last year, Commander Wú (吳公) sucked her father’s carbuncle,
and her father fought without turning back,
and consequently died at the hands of the enemy.
Commander Wú (吳公) has now again sucked her son’s carbuncle,
and I do not know where he will die,

1 There was a solar eclipse.
Dù Yù (杜預) says: "The sun moves slowly,
completing one celestial circuit in a year.
The moon moves quickly,
completing one celestial circuit in a month;
in a year there are twelve conjunctions in total."
"However, the sun and moon are
moving bodies.
Although their orbital speed has a general measure,
they cannot but have minor gains or losses,
hence there are cases where they conjunct but do not eclipse,
or where they conjunct frequently and eclipse."
Kǒng Yǐngdá (孔穎達) says: "The conjunction of the sun and moon
is called the new moon."
"A celestial circuit is three hundred sixty-five and a quarter degrees."
Both the sun and moon move clockwise in the sky.
In one day and one night, the sun moves one degree,
and the moon moves thirteen and seven-nineteenths degrees.
After twenty-nine days and a remainder,
the moon completes one celestial circuit,
catches up with the sun, and conjuncts with it.
If at conjunction the sun and moon are on the same path, there is an eclipse;
if the moon is outside or inside the sun's path,
then there is no eclipse."
"Furthermore, calendrical experts have a method for eclipses,
roughly setting the limit at one hundred seventy-three days and a remainder."
"However, if the moon is first on the inside,
then eclipses occurring according to the limit are many;
if the moon is on the outside,
then eclipses occurring according to the limit are few."
Dù Yù (杜預) observed these discrepancies,
and therefore said:
"Although their orbital speed has a general measure,
they cannot but have minor gains or losses,
hence there are cases where they conjunct but do not eclipse,
or where they conjunct frequently and eclipse."
This is correct.
Sū Shì (蘇氏) says: "When conjunction occurs at the new moon, there is a solar eclipse,
but there are also cases of conjunction without an eclipse."
"When conjunction leads to an eclipse, it means *yáng* (陽) is weak and *yīn* (陰) prevails over it;
when conjunction does not lead to an eclipse, it means *yáng* (陽) is strong and *yīn* (陰) cannot obscure it."
Zhū Yuánhuì (朱元晦) says: "This is related to the influence of human affairs."
"If subjects betray their lords,
concubines dominate their husbands,
petty people oppress gentlemen,
and barbarians invade the Middle Kingdom,
such influences cause *yīn* (陰) to prevail and *yáng* (陽) to weaken, leading to a solar eclipse."
"Thus, the sages in the *Chūnqiū* (春秋)
always recorded every eclipse,
and the poets also considered it an ill omen."
"This text only records the year but not the month, last day, or new moon,
which is an omission by the historian."
The Shìmíng (釋名) says: "The waning of the sun and moon is called *shí* (食, to eat);
a gradual, small diminishing,
like insects eating the leaves of plants."

Rú Chún said: When the Son of Heaven marries his daughter to a feudal lord,
he must appoint a member of the feudal lord's own clan to preside over the ceremony,
hence she is called Gōngzhǔ (公主, literally "Duke's Hostess" or "Public Hostess").
An imperial sister is called Chánggōngzhǔ (長公主, Eldest Princess),
and a daughter of a prince is called Wēngzhǔ (翁主, literally "Elder's Hostess" or "Father's Hostess").
Shī Gǔ said: Rú's explanation is correct.
The Son of Heaven does not personally preside over the marriage,
hence she is called Gōngzhǔ;
whereas princes do personally preside over their daughters' marriages,
hence their daughters are called Wēngzhǔ.
Wēng
means father,
indicating that the father presides over her marriage;
she is also called Wángzhǔ (王主, literally "King's Hostess"),
indicating that the king personally presides over her marriage.
Yáng Xióng's Fāngyán states: The people of Zhōu, Jìn, Qín, and Lǒng call father 'wēng'.

Liú Gòngfù said: I believe the term Gōngzhǔ originally came from old Qín customs,
where a son was a Gōngzǐ (公子, duke's son),
and a daughter was a Gōngzhǔ.
In ancient times, the wife of a Dàfū (大夫, high official) was called Zhǔ (主, hostess),
so 'gōng' was paired with it.
If it is said that someone of the same clan presided over it,
hence she was called Gōngzhǔ,
then that was a custom of Zhōu,
and Qín would not have known to use it.
In ancient times, when marrying off a daughter,
according to the rites, a Dàfū should have presided over it, as in Zhōu;
why wasn't she called Fūzhǔ (夫主)?
Therefore, those called Wángzhǔ
are like calling them Wángzǐ (王子, king's son);
those called Gōngzhǔ
simply originated from 'gōng'.

Wéngōng 文公 died in his twenty-third year.
In the twenty-fourth year of Qǐnggōng 頃公, Chǔ 楚 extinguished Lǔ 魯.
Bān Gù's 班固 *Hàn Shū Lǜlì Zhì* 漢書律曆志
writes "Wéngōng" 文公
as
"Míngōng" 緡公.
The only difference in the years of their reigns compared to the *Shìjiā* is
Pínggōng 平公's twenty years.
This chronicle, starting from the winter solstice on the first day of the first month, *xīnhài* 辛亥, in the fifth year of Lǔ Xīgōng 魯僖公,
up to the winter solstice on the first day of the first month, *gēngyín* 庚寅, in the twelfth year of Chénggōng 成公;
the winter solstice on the first day of the first month, *jǐsì* 己巳, in the seventh year of Dìnggōng 定公;
the winter solstice on the first day of the first month, *wùshēn* 戊申, in the fourth year of Yuángōng 元公;
the winter solstice on the first day of the first month, *dīnghài* 丁亥, in the fourth year of Kānggōng 康公;
the winter solstice on the first day of the first month, *bǐngyín* 丙寅, in the twenty-second year of Míngōng 緡公;
the winter solstice on the first day of the eleventh month, *yǐsì* 乙巳, in the eighth year of Hàn Gāozǔ 漢高祖;
and the winter solstice on the first day of the eleventh month, *jiǎshēn* 甲申, in the sixth year of Wǔdì Yuánshuò 武帝元朔;
the winter solstice on the first day of the eleventh month, *guǐhài* 癸亥, in the second year of Yuándì Chūyuán 元帝初元—
the intervals between them are all seventy-six years.
This is the most accurate,
and also consistent with the annotations in the *Lǔ Shìjiā* and the chronological records by Huángfǔ Mì 皇甫謐.
We follow this now.
The *Liùguóbiǎo* is somewhat erroneous,
and cannot be fully relied upon.
I note that the *Kǎoyì* states,
"From the fifth year of Lǔ Xīgōng 魯僖公 to the second year of Hàn Yuándì Chūyuán 漢元帝初元, over six hundred years,
the winter solstices on the first day of the twelfth month [or first month, as given above]
are all seventy-six years apart.
This is the most accurate,
and also consistent with the annotations in the *Lǔ Shìjiā* and the chronological records by Huángfǔ Mì 皇甫謐."
This probably refers to Liú Yīsǒu's 劉彞叟 *Chánglì* 長曆 (Long Calendar).
It also says,
"The *Shǐjì Liùguóbiǎo* 史記六國表 is somewhat erroneous,
and cannot be fully relied upon."
Furthermore, the chronological table in the *Tōngjiàn Mùlù* 通鑑目錄 uses Liú Yīsǒu's 劉彞叟 *Chánglì* 長曆.
In the first year of Hàn Wǔdì Tàichū 漢武帝太初,
the Xià Summer calendar was first used to fix the calendar.
The *Shǐjì Lìshū* 史記曆書 records *ēfēng shè Tígé* 閼逢攝提格 for this year,
while the catalogue records *qiángyǔ chìfènruò* 強圉赤奮若.
*Ēfēng shè Tígé* 閼逢攝提格
is *jiǎyín* 甲寅,
while *qiángyǔ chìfènruò* 強圉赤奮若
is *dīngchǒu* 丁丑,
a difference of twenty-four years.
Wēngōng 溫公 used Yīsǒu's 彞叟 calendar,
and Shào Kāngjié's 邵康節 *Huángjí Jīngshì Shū* 皇極經世書 also used Yīsǒu's 彞叟 calendar.
Kāngjié 康節 initially prided himself on his talent;
after he began his studies,
he strenuously pursued lofty and distant goals.
Upon meeting Lǐ Zhīcái 李之才,
he followed him and received instruction,
living in a hut in Báiyuán 百源, Gòngchéng 共城.
He did not use a stove in winter,
nor a fan in summer,
and for several years did not lie down on a mat at night,
pondering deeply on the *Yìjīng* 易經.
The *Huángjí Jīngshì Shū* could not deviate from Yīsǒu's 彞叟 calendar.
When he came to live in Luò 洛, Wēngōng 溫公 also held a ceremonial post,
and as the publishing bureau was in Luò 洛,
they frequently visited each other,
and Kāngjié 康節 was also someone Wēngōng 溫公 had long respected.
I believe that in their discussions, this matter must have been raised,
and it was decided to use Yīsǒu's 彞叟 calendar.
Reading this section of the *Kǎoyì*,
the meaning of the words is clear.
4 Hán Wénhóu 韓文侯 薨,
his son Āihóu 哀侯 was enthroned.
1 The King collapsed,
his son Lièwáng Xǐ 烈王喜 was enthroned.
2 Wèi 魏, Hán 韓, and Zhào 趙 jointly deposed Jìn Jìnggōng 晉靖公 as a commoner and divided his territory.
Tángshū 唐叔 no longer received sacrifices.
Lièwáng 烈王
was named Xǐ 喜,
Anwáng's 安王 son.
1 There was a solar eclipse.
2 Hán 韓 extinguished Zhèng 鄭,
and consequently moved its capital there.
Hán 韓 originally had its capital in Píngyáng 平陽,
its territory belonging to Hàn's 漢 Hédōng Jùn 河東郡;
later it moved its capital to Yángzhái 陽翟.
Zhèng 鄭 had its capital in Xīnzhèng 新鄭,
its territory belonging to Hàn's 漢 Hénán Jùn 河南郡.
Zhèng Huángōng 鄭桓公 was first enfeoffed in Zhèng 鄭,
its territory belonging to Hàn's 漢 Jīngzhào 京兆;
later it extinguished Guó 虢 and Kuài 鄶 and established its state between the Zhēn 溱 and Wěi 洧 rivers,
hence it was called Xīnzhèng 新鄭.
This is what *Zuǒzhuàn* 左傳 refers to when Zhèng Zhuānggōng 鄭莊公 said,
"Our former ruler established a new city here."
Now that Hán 韓 had extinguished Zhèng 鄭,
it moved its capital there from Yángzhái 陽翟.
Since Hán 韓 made Zhèng 鄭 its capital,
people at the time also referred to the King of Hán 韓 as the King of Zhèng 鄭.
This can be seen by consulting the *Zhànguócè* 戰國策 and *Hán Fēizǐ* 韓非子.
3 Zhào Jìnghóu 趙敬侯 薨,
his son Chénghóu Zhǒng 成侯種 was enthroned.
1 Yān 燕 defeated the Qí 齊 army at Línhú 林狐.
Lǔ 魯 attacked Qí 齊,
entering Yángguān 陽關.
Xú Guǎng 徐廣 said: Yángguān 陽關 is in Jùpíng 鉅平.
Bān Zhì's 班志 states: Jùpíng Xiàn 鉅平縣 belongs to Tàishān Jùn 泰山郡.
The *Kuòdì Zhì* 括地志 states: The old city of Yángguān 陽關 is twenty-nine *lǐ* to the south of Bóchéng Xiàn 博城縣 in Yǎnzhōu 兗州.
The west side of its city borders the Wénshuǐ 汶水.
Wén 汶
is pronounced wèn.
Wèi 魏 attacked Qí 齊,
reaching Bólíng 博陵.
The *Shǐjì Zhèngyì* 史記正義 says: Bólíng 博陵 is on the western border of Jìzhōu 濟州.
Sòng Bái 宋白 says: The *Shǐjì* states,
Qí Wēiwáng 齊威王 attacked Jìn 晉 reaching Bólíng 博陵.
Xú Guǎng 徐廣 says: Bópíng 博平 of Dōngjùn 東郡 became a county during the Hàn 漢 dynasty.
2 Yān Xīgōng 燕僖公 薨,
his son Huángōng 桓公 was enthroned.
3 Sòng Xiūgōng 宋休公 薨,
his son Pìgōng 辟公 was enthroned.
Pì 辟 is also not recorded in the posthumous naming rules.
4 Wèi Shèngōng 衞慎公 薨,
his son Shēnggōng Xùn 聲公訓 was enthroned.
According to the posthumous naming rules: "Shèn" refers to one who is keen and respectful.
The *Dàijì* 戴記 says: "Shèn" refers to one whose thoughts are profound and far-reaching.
1 Zhào 趙 attacked Wèi 衞,
taking seventy-three of its capital districts (*dūbǐ*) 都鄙.
*Zhōulǐ* 周禮 states: The Grand Tutor governs capital districts (*dūbǐ*) by eight rules.
The commentary says: The area where a capital (*dū*) is located is called a *bǐ* 鄙.
*Dūbǐ* 都鄙 refers to the fiefs of high ministers and grand masters.
According to the Zhōu 周 system, four counties formed a capital (*dū*),
forty *lǐ* square,
with one thousand six hundred fields (*jǐng*),
accumulating fourteen thousand four hundred men.
Five *zǎn* 酇 formed a *bǐ* 鄙,
a *bǐ* 鄙 having five hundred households.
At this time, the state of Wèi 衞 was small.
If it had seventy-three *dūbǐ* 都鄙,
applying the system of the flourishing Zhōu 周, its territory would be vast.
Even the entire registered land of Wèi 衞
might not reach this number.
Further extensive research is needed.
2 Wèi 魏 defeated the Zhào 趙 army at Běilìn 北藺.
Bān Zhì's 班志 states: Xīhé Jùn 西河郡 has Lìn Xiàn 藺縣.
The *Shǐjì Zhèngyì* 史記正義 says: It is in Shízhōu 石州.
Its location relative to Zhào 趙 was to the northwest,
hence it was called Běilìn 北藺 (North Lìn).
Lìn 藺
is pronounced *lǐnjìn* 離進.
1 Wèi 魏 attacked Chǔ 楚,
taking Lǔyáng 魯陽.
This is the "Lú Xiàn" 魯縣 to which Liú Lěi 劉累 moved, as mentioned in the *Zuǒzhuàn* 左傳,
which is Lǔyáng 魯陽.
Bān Zhì's 班志 states: Lǔyáng Xiàn 魯陽縣 belongs to Nányáng Jùn 南陽郡.
The *Shǐjì Zhèngyì* 史記正義 says: It is present-day Lǔshān Xiàn 魯山縣 in Rǔzhōu 汝州.
2. Hán Yánsuì (韓嚴遂) assassinated Àihóu (哀侯).
The people of the state enthroned his son, Yìhóu (懿侯).
Originally,
Àihóu had appointed Hán Kuǐ (韓廆) as prime minister, but he favored Yánsuì.
The two greatly harmed each other.
Yánsuì ordered someone to assassinate Hán Kuǐ in the court.
Kuǐ ran to Àihóu.
Àihóu embraced him.
The assassin who attacked Hán Kuǐ
also struck Àihóu.
The *Zhànguócè* (戰國策) treats the assassination of Hán's prime minister by Niè Zhèng (聶政) and the simultaneous striking of Àihóu as one event.
This passage follows the *Shǐjì* (史記).
A note in the Shǔ (蜀) edition says: According to the Grand Historian's *Niánbiǎo* (年表) and *Hán Shìjiā* (韓世家),
in the third year of Hán Lièhóu (韓烈侯), both record
"Niè Zhèng killed Hán's prime minister Xiálěi (俠累),"
and in the sixth year of Àihóu, both record
"Yánsuì assassinated Àihóu."
Examining this with the *Cìkè Zhuàn* (刺客傳),
Niè Zhèng's killing of Xiálěi occurred during Àihóu's time.
Examining it with the *Zhànguócè* also yields the same conclusion.
Following the *Zhuàn* and the *Zhànguócè*,
then the *Niánbiǎo* and *Shìjiā*'s record in the third year of Lièhóu of
"a bandit killed Xiálěi"
is erroneous.
The *Tōngjiàn* (通鑑) records Niè Zhèng's killing of Xiálěi in the third year of Lièhóu,
and then records Yánsuì's killing of his lord Àihóu in the sixth year of Àihóu.
This follows what is recorded in the *Niánbiǎo* and *Shìjiā*.
Perhaps the *Cìkè Zhuàn* initially did not mention the simultaneous killing of Àihóu,
and only the *Zhànguócè* mentioned it.
Could the *Tōngjiàn* have doubted this?
Therefore, it records the simultaneous stabbing of Àihóu,
but does not mention Niè Zhèng,
only saying
"sent someone."
Seeking the reason for this,
the intention of the *Tōngjiàn* is not to equate Yán Zhòngzǐ (嚴仲子) with Yánsuì,
nor to equate Xiálěi with Hán Kuǐ,
but rather to follow the *Niánbiǎo* and *Shìjiā* and not believe their *Zhuàn*.
I note that Wēn Gōng (溫公) in his letter to Liú Dàoyuán (劉道原) also doubted this matter.
Kuǐ (廆):
Pronounced as "hù huì fān."
Xiàng (相):
Pronounced as "xī liàng fān."
Cì (刺):
Pronounced as "qī yì fān."
Cháo (朝):
Pronounced as "zhí yáo fān."
Zǒu (走):
Pronounced "zòu."
3. Wèi Wǔhóu (魏武侯) passed away.
No heir apparent was established.
His son, Yīng (罃), and Gōngzhōng Huǎn (公中緩) contended for the throne,
causing chaos in the state.
1. Qí Wēiwáng (齊威王) came to pay homage to the court.
At this time, the Zhōu (周) house was weak,
and no feudal lords paid homage,
but Qí alone paid homage.
The world thereby increasingly esteemed Wēiwáng as virtuous.
2. Zhào (趙) attacked Qí,
reaching Juàn (鄄).
The *Bān Zhì* (班志) states that Jìyīn Jùn (濟陰郡) has Juànchéng Xiàn (鄄城縣).
Juàn (鄄):
Pronounced as "gōng yuàn fān."
3. Wèi (魏) defeated the Zhào army at Huái (懷).
The *Bān Zhì* states that Hénèi Jùn (河內郡) has Huái Xiàn (懷縣).
Wèi Shōu's (魏收) *Dìxíng Zhì* (地形志) states that Huáizhōu (懷州) Wǔdé Jùn (武德郡) has Huái Xiàn,
and within the county there is Huáichéng (懷城).
Bài (敗):
Pronounced as "bǔ mài fān."
4. Qí Wēiwáng summoned the Grand Administrator of Jìmò (即墨),
and said to him:
"Since you took up residence in Jìmò,
negative reports have arrived daily."
The *Bān Zhì* states that Jìmò Xiàn (即墨縣) belonged to Jiāodōng Guó (膠東國).
The *Kuòdì Zhì* (括地志) states: The old city of Jìmò
is sixty *lǐ* south of Jiāoshuǐ Xiàn (膠水縣) in Láizhōu (萊州).
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: The city borders the Mòshuǐ (墨水) river,
hence it is called Jìmò.
Yǔ (語):
Pronounced as "niú jù fān";
the same below.
"The fields are cultivated,
the people are self-sufficient,
the officials have no troubles,
and the East is peaceful.
This is because you did not seek help from my close attendants!"
He enfeoffed him with ten thousand households.
He summoned the Grand Administrator of Ā (阿),
and said to him:
"Since you have guarded Ā,
reports of praise have arrived daily."
Ā (阿):
refers to Dōng'ā Xiàn (東阿縣);
the *Bān Zhì* states it belonged to Dōng Jùn (東郡).
Yù (譽):
Pronounced "yú,"
meaning to commend its beauty.
"The fields are not cultivated,
and the people are poor and hungry.
Formerly, when Zhào attacked Juàn,
you did not rescue it.
When Wèi (衞) took Xuēlín (薛陵),
you did not know."
Xuēlín (薛陵):
was the ruins of the state of Xuē (薛) during the Spring and Autumn period.
The *Bān Dì* (班地) states that Xuē Xiàn (薛縣) belonged to Lǔ Guó (魯國),
while the state of Wèi (衞) was in the Hán Dōng Jùn (漢東郡) Chénliú (陳留) area.
Xuēlín belonged to Qí but was close to Wèi (衞),
hence it was taken by them.
Later, Qí enfeoffed Tián Yīng (田嬰) here.
On this day,
he boiled the Grand Administrator of Ā and the close attendants who had previously praised him.
Thereupon, all the officials were filled with dread,
no one dared to feign or deceive,
and they strove to reveal their true feelings.
The state of Qí was greatly governed,
and became powerful in the world.
5. Chǔ Sùwáng (楚肅王) passed away.
Having no son,
his younger brother Liángfū (良夫) was enthroned,
who was Xuānwáng (宣王).
6. Sòng Pìgōng (宋辟公) passed away.
His son Tìchén (剔成) was enthroned.
1. There was a solar eclipse.
2. The king passed away.
His younger brother Biǎn (扁) was enthroned,
who was Xiǎnwáng (顯王).
3. Wèi's Grand Master, Wáng Cuò (王錯), fled to Hán.
The *Xìngpǔ* (姓譜) states: The origins of the Wáng (王) clan are not singular.
Those from Tàiyuán (太原) and Lángyá (琅邪) are descendants of Zhōu Língwáng's (周靈王) crown prince Jìn (晉).
Běihǎi (北海) and Chénliú (陳留) are descendants of Qí Wáng Tián Hé (齊王田和).
Dōnghǎi (東海) originated from the Jī (姬) surname.
Gāopíng (高平) and Jīngzhào (京兆) are descendants of Wèi Xìnlíngjūn (魏信陵君).

Those from Tiānshuǐ (天水), Dōngpíng (東平), Xīncài (新蔡), Xīnyě (新野), Shānyáng (山陽), Zhōngshān (中山), Zhāngwǔ (章武), Dōnglái (東萊), and Hédōng (河東) are from Yīn (殷) Prince Bǐ Gān (比干), who was harmed by Zhòu (紂);
his descendants, being of royal lineage,
were called the Wáng clan.
I believe these all refer to the prominent clans of various commanderies in later generations.
During the Spring and Autumn period, there was already the Wáng surname,
but its origin cannot be ascertained.
"Wèi is in chaos,
it can be seized."
Gōngsūn (公孫): a surname.
The Yellow Emperor,
Gōngsūn clan.
Qí (頎):
Pronounced as "qú xī fān."
They fought at Zhuózé (濁澤),
greatly defeating them,
and then besieged Wèi.
The *Shǐjì Zhèngyì* (史記正義) says: Xú Guǎng (徐廣) thought it was Chángshè (長社) Zhuózé,
which is incorrect.
The *Kuòdì Zhì* states: The Zhuóshuǐ (濁水) river originates from the flat ground northeast of Xiè Xiàn (解縣) in Púzhōu (蒲州).
At that time, Wèi's capital was Ānyì (安邑).
How could Hán and Zhào, in attacking Wèi, have reached Chángshè in Hénán (河南)?
The Zhuóshuǐ in Xiè Xiàn is close to Wèi's capital,
so it should be that.
"Kill Yīng,
enthrone Gōngzhōng Huǎn,
carve up the territory and withdraw.
This is beneficial for our two states."
Yìhóu said:
"This is unacceptable.
To kill the lord of Wèi is tyrannical;
to carve up territory and withdraw is greedy.
It is better to divide it into two.
If Wèi is divided into two,
it will be no stronger than Sòng (宋) or Wèi (衞),
then we will ultimately have no worries from Wèi."
The Zhào people did not listen.
Yìhóu was displeased,
and left with his troops overnight.
Zhào Chénghóu (趙成侯) also left.
Yīng then killed Gōngzhōng Huǎn and was enthroned,
who was Huìwáng (惠王).
Grand Scribe Tàishǐgōng said: The reason why King Huì of Wèi himself did not die and his state was not divided
was that the two states' plans were not in agreement.
If they had followed the plan of one party,
Wèi would certainly have been divided.
Therefore, it is said:
"If a ruler dies
and has no legitimate son (dízi),
his state can be shattered."
Suǒyǐn says: This is probably an ancient saying or a popular saying,
so it says
"Therefore, it is said".
'適' (shì)
is read as '嫡' (dí).
Collated by Qí Sīhé and punctuated by Gù Jiégāng and Niè Chóngqí.
Your servant, Cháosàn Dàfū, Yòu Jiànyì Dàfū, Quán Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng, Chōng Lǐjiǎn Shǐ, Shàng Hùjūn, who was bestowed with the purple and gold fish-pouch,
by imperial decree, compiled this.
Hòu Xué Tiāntái
Xiǎnwáng
The "Methods of Posthumous Titles" of eleven families: "His actions are seen both within and without" is called Xiǎn;
"He received blessings from Heaven" is called Xiǎn;
"All the lords took him as their model" is called Xiǎn.
It seems that Duke Zhōugōng did not have this posthumous title,
but in the late period of Zhōu, King Xiǎn was posthumously titled Xiǎn.
This suggests that later generations who copied Duke Zhōugōng's posthumous titles omitted it.
1. Qí attacked Wèi,
and took Guānjīn.
Kāng says: Qí attacked Wèi,
and King Huì of Wèi requested to offer Guān to make peace,
which is Guānjīn.
I note that Bān Zhì records Guānjīn County in Xìndū Commandery,
which is very far from Qí,
and is also Zhào territory.
Also, Dōngjùn had Pànguān County.
Shuǐ Jīng says: The old channel of the Dàhé River flows east past the wilderness of Wǔlù,
and then east past the south of the old city of Wèiguó,
which was ancient Zhēnguān.
Is this Wèi's Guānjīn?
Xú Guǎng says: Guān
is modern Wèi County.
Shǐ Jì Zhèngyì says: Guānchéng County in Wèizhōu
was the ancient state of Guān.
Guó Yǔ says: Guān state
was the fief of the fifth younger brother of Xià Tàikāng.
Guān is pronounced Gōng Huàn fān.
2. Zhào invaded Qí,
and took Chángchéng.
Liú Zhāozhì says: Lú County in Jìběi has Chángchéng.
Shǐ Jì records Sū Dài persuading the King of Yān saying:
"Qí has Chángchéng and Jùfáng,"
which refers to this.
1. Wèi and Hán met at Zháiyáng.
Shuǐ Jīng Zhù says: There is Shāchéng at the edge of Xíngzé,
commonly called Shuǐchéng,
which is incorrect. Wèi Rǎn fled from Mángmǎo,
and entered Běizhái,
which is this Zháiyáng City.
Kuòdì Zhì says: The old city of Zháiyáng
is seventeen lǐ east of Xíngyáng County, Zhèngzhōu.
2. Qín defeated the Wèi and Hán armies at Luòyáng.
Luòyáng is north of the Luò River;
Duke Zhōugōng moved the Yīn people here
and called it Chéngzhōu.
Bān Zhì, it belonged to Hénán Commandery.
'敗' (bài) is pronounced Bǔ Mài fān.
1. Wèi attacked Sòng.

Mò (沫) and Guì (劌) are close in sound but different in character.
These four rulers were not purely virtuous in their ways,
and Shāng Jūn (商君) was especially known for being harsh and cruel.
Moreover, living in an era of warfare,
when the world was inclined towards deceit and force,
they still dared not forget trust to nurture their people.
How much more so should those who govern the world in peace and order!
Hán Yì Hóu (韓懿侯) passed away,
and his son Zhāo Hóu (昭侯) ascended the throne.
Shì Fǎ (諡法) says: "Zhāo" (昭) means virtuous and meritorious;
"Zhāo" (昭) means renowned and far-reaching in wisdom.
Qín (秦) defeated the Hán (韓) army at Xīshān (西山).
From Yíyáng (宜陽) and Xióng'ěr (熊耳) eastward to Sōnggāo (嵩高),
and south to Lǔyáng (魯陽),
all were Hán's (韓) Xīshān (西山).
敗 (bài),
pronounced as Bǔ-mài.
Wèi (魏) and Hán (韓)
met at Kuò (鄗).
Bān Zhì (班志) states that Kuò (鄗) County belonged to Zhōngshān (中山) Commandery.
At this time, it was Zhào (趙) territory;
in the Later Hàng (後漢), it was renamed Gāoyì (高邑),
and in the Táng (唐), it was the land of Báixiāng (柏鄉) County and Zànhuáng (贊皇) County in Zhàozhōu (趙州).
Kuò (鄗),
pronounced as Hū-gè.
Zhào (趙) and Yān (燕) met at Ā (阿).
Zhào (趙), Qí (齊), and Sòng (宋) met at Pínglù (平陸).
1 Qí Wēiwáng and Wèi Huìwáng met for a hunt in the suburbs.
Huìwáng said,
“Does Qí also have treasures?”
Wēiwáng said,
“No, we do not.”
Huìwáng said,
“Although my state is small,
I still have ten pearls, each an inch in diameter,
that illuminate twelve chariots in front and twelve in back.
How can a great state like Qí be without treasures?”
Wēiwáng said,
“What I consider treasures differs from what Your Majesty considers treasures.
I have an official named Tánzǐ.
The Xìngpǔ (Genealogical Record) says: a ducal clan of Qí was enfeoffed in Tánchéng, Xiáqiū,
and thus took Tán as their surname.
The city was on the southern border of Qí,
hence it was called Nánchéng (South City).
The twelve feudal lords along the Sì River all came to pay homage.
I have an official named Pànzǐ,
whom I sent to guard Gāotáng,
and then the people of Zhào dared not fish east of the Hé River.
I have an officer named Qiánfū,
whom I sent to guard Xúzhōu,
and then the people of Yān sacrificed at the north gate,
and the people of Zhào sacrificed at the west gate.
Yān is to the north of Qí,
and Zhào is to the west of Qí.
Jiǎ Kuí says: Yān and Zhào feared Qí,
hence they sacrificed to seek blessings.
Yān,
pronounced ‘jiān fān.’
I have an official named Zhǒngshǒu,
whom I appointed to guard against bandits and thieves,
and then nothing was picked up from the roads.
These four officials
can illuminate a thousand *lǐ*,
how could it be merely twelve chariots!”
Huìwáng showed a look of shame.
2 Qín Xiàogōng and Wèi Huìwáng met at Dùpíng.
The Bānzhì (Record of Divisions) says:
In Jīngzhào there was Dùlíng County,
which was the state of Dùbó of ancient Zhōu.
The Shǐjì Guàn Yīng Zhuàn (Biography of Guàn Yīng in the Records of the Grand Historian) says: Yīng, as Marquis of Chāngpíng, received his fief in Dùpíng Township.
Zhèngyì says: Dùpíng is in the vicinity of Chéngchéng County, Tóngzhōu in Táng.
The Wèi Shìjiā (Hereditary House of Wèi) writes it as
“Shèpíng.”
3 Lǔ Gònggōng passed away,
and his son Kānggōng Máo was enthroned.
1 Qín defeated the Wèi army at Yuánlǐ.
The Shǐjì Zhèngyì says: Yuánlǐ is also in the vicinity of Chéngchéng County, Tóngzhōu.
Bài,
pronounced ‘bǔ mài fān.’
According to Qín law, a warrior who decapitated an enemy in battle
was granted one rank of nobility,
hence it was called ‘jí’ (rank/head).
2 Wèi Huìwáng attacked Zhào,
besieging Hándān.
The King of Chǔ sent Jǐng Shě to rescue Zhào.
1 Qí Wēiwáng sent Tián Jì to rescue Zhào.
Originally,
Sūn Bìn and Páng Juàn both studied military strategy.
The Xìngpǔ says: Kāngshú Fēng, son of King Wén of Zhōu, was enfeoffed in Wèi.
Down to Wǔgōngzǐ Huìsūn Zēng'ěr, who was a senior minister of Wèi,
and thus took Sūn as his surname.
Later there were Sūn Wǔ and Sūn Bìn,
both skilled in military matters.

Zhào Míngchéng’s Jīnshílù (Record of Inscriptions on Metal and Stone) has a stele of Sūn Gēn, Administrator of Ānpíng during the Hàn dynasty, which says: The ancestors originally came from a descendant of the Yīn dynasty.
When King Wǔ pacified Zhōu,
he sealed the tomb of Bǐ Gān,
and his descendants split and spread,
then settled on Sūn as their surname.
The Xìngpǔ also says: The Páng surname
comes from the descendants of Bì Gōng Gāo;
a branch was enfeoffed in Páng,
and thus took Páng as their surname.
Bìn,
pronounced ‘pín rěn fān,’
refers to the punishment of *yuè* (amputation),
removing the kneecaps.
Zhèng Xuán says: Zhōu changed *bìn* to *yuè*;
*yuè* means cutting off the foot.
The Shūzhuàn (Book of Documents and Commentaries) says: for those who broke through passes and bridges, or scaled city walls and plundered,
the punishment was *bìn*.
Sūn Bìn was likely called *Bìn* because of his amputated feet.
The Shuōwén says: *Bìn* refers to
the end of the knee;
the Lèipiān says: pronounced ‘pí bīn qiè.’
Páng,
pronounced ‘bó jiāng fān.’
Juàn,
pronounced ‘gǔ xuán fān.’
The office of general
has existed since the Zhōu dynasty.
Then he was summoned;
when he arrived,
by law, both his feet were amputated and he was tattooed (qíng),
intending to cripple him for life.
When a Qí envoy arrived in Wèi,
Sūn Bìn secretly met him as a criminal,
and spoke to the Qí envoy;
the Qí envoy secretly took him in his carriage to Qí.
Zhī,
means to go.
He was presented to Wēiwáng.
Wēiwáng questioned him about military strategy,
and thereupon made him his master.
Thus Wēiwáng planned to rescue Zhào,
making Sūn Bìn the general;
he declined, saying that a person with a disabled body was unsuitable,
so Tián Jì was made general and Master Sūn the strategist,
residing in a supply wagon,
sitting and devising strategies.
Tián Jì wanted to lead his troops to Zhào.
Master Sūn said:
“To untangle something convoluted and tangled, one does not clench one’s fist.”
Suǒyǐn says: This refers to matters that are complicated and tangled.
To untangle something convoluted and tangled,
one should skillfully use one’s hand to untangle it,
not clench one’s fist and strike it.
I say that “convoluted and tangled” refers to people fighting,
not to matters.
Kāng says: Quán (fist)
is the same as juàn.
Juàn is the rope used to tie up sleeves.
I say we should follow the Suǒyǐn’s explanation,
Kāng’s explanation is incorrect.
Fú,
pronounced ‘fú.’
Attack the strong points, strike the weak points;
when their formation is disrupted and their momentum checked,
they will naturally unravel.
Now Liáng and Zhào are attacking each other;
their light troops and elite soldiers must be exhausted externally,
and the old and weak internally.
You would do better to lead your troops swiftly to the capital of Wèi,
occupy its main roads,
and strike at its vulnerable points.
They will surely abandon Zhào to save themselves: this way, with one move, we relieve the siege of Zhào and take advantage of Wèi’s exhaustion.”
Tián Jì followed his advice.
In the tenth month,
Hándān surrendered to Wèi.
The Wèi army returned
and fought Qí at Guìlíng,
where the Wèi army suffered a great defeat.
2 Hán attacked Dōngzhōu,
taking Língguān and Lǐnqīu.
The Zhōu court was in decline;
during the Warring States period, it had only seven towns:
Hénán, Luòyáng, Gǔchéng, Píngyīn, Yǎnshī, Gǒng, and Gōushì in Hàn times.
The Jìnzhì says: King Kǎo of Zhōu enfeoffed Gōngzǐ Huìgōng, grandson of Duke Huán of Zhōu, in Gǒng,
and he was called Duke of Dōngzhōu.
Hence, during the Warring States period, there were Dōngzhōu and Xīzhōu,
with Mángshān and Shǒushān as their borders.
Língguān and Lǐnqīu are names of towns at that time;
there is no record in historical texts.
Lǐnqīu
is written as
“Xíngqīu” in the Shǐjì.
Guān,
pronounced ‘gǔ wán fān.’
3 Chǔ Zhāo Xīxù became prime minister.
Jiāng Yǐ spoke to the King of Chǔ, saying:
“There was a man who loved his dog.
The dog once fell into a well.
Zhāo, Qū, Jǐng,
are powerful clans of Chǔ,
known as
‘Sānlǘ’ (Three Clans).
Tàishǐgōng (Grand Historian) says: The Yíng surname branched out to become the Jiāng clan.
Xiàng,
pronounced ‘xī liàng fān.’
Nì,
pronounced ‘nú diào fān.’
When he wanted to go in and tell him,
the dog stood at the gate and bit him.
Now Zhāo Xīxù constantly dislikes my presence;
it is just like this.
Furthermore, if a person is fond of praising others’ good deeds,
Your Majesty says, ‘This is a gentleman,’
and draws near to him;
if he is fond of proclaiming others’ bad deeds,
Your Majesty says, ‘This is a petty man,’
and keeps him at a distance.
However, there will be sons who murder their fathers, and ministers who murder their lords,
and Your Majesty will never know.
Why?
Because Your Majesty likes to hear of people’s good deeds but dislikes to hear of people’s bad deeds.”
The King said,
“Excellent,
I wish to hear both.”
Jiāng Yǐ wished to slander Zhāo Xīxù, hence he first made this statement.
1 Qín's Dàliángzào attacked Wèi.
Suǒyǐn says: Dàliángzào
is Dàshàngzào.
I say that Dàliángzào
is the best among Dàshàngzào.
According to the "Records of the Grand Historian," "Annals of Qín": In the tenth year of Xiàogōng,
Wèi Yāng became Dàliángzào,
led troops to besiege Wèi's Ānyì,
and captured it.
Also according to the "Chronological Tables of the Six States,"
in the tenth year of Qín Xiàogōng
and the seventeenth year of Xiǎnwáng,
the so-called Dàliángzào attacking Wèi
refers to Wèi Yāng leading troops.
At that time, Wèi's capital was Ānyì,
and its army was still strong.
Páng Juàn, Crown Prince Shēn, and Gōngzǐ Áng had not yet been defeated,
so Ānyì should not have surrendered to Qín so quickly.
It was not until the twenty-ninth year of Xiǎnwáng,
after Áng's army was defeated,
that Wèi offered the land west of the Hé to Qín,
and only then did it leave Ānyì and move its capital to Dàliáng.
The "Chronological Tables of the Six States" does not record the move to Dàliáng, but the "Hereditary Houses" does.
The "Hereditary House of Wèi" does not record Ānyì surrendering to Qín in that year, but the "Annals of Qín" records it in the tenth year of Xiàogōng.
The "Zīzhì Tōngjiàn" follows the "Hereditary House of Wèi,"
recording Wèi leaving Ānyì
and moving to Dàliáng in the twenty-ninth year of Xiǎnwáng,
and not recording Ānyì surrendering to Qín in that year,
probably also due to doubt and thus removing it.
But after Dàliángzào, there should be
the two characters
"Wèi Yāng,"
meaning that the transcribers of the "Zīzhì Tōngjiàn" omitted them.
[Zhāng: The twelve-line edition indeed has
the two characters
"Wèi Yāng";
the eighteen-line edition is the same;
the Kǒng edition is the same;
Tuìzhāi's collation is the same.]
2 The feudal lords besieged Wèi at Xiānglíng.
The "Records of the Grand Historian: Corrected Meanings" says: The old city of Xiānglíng
is in Zōuxiàn, Yǎnzhōu.
I note that Wèi's territory at that time did not extend to Zōu.
In the "History of the Former Hàn Dynasty: Monograph on Geography,"
Hédōng had Xiānglíng County.
Shīgǔ says: The tomb of Jìn Xiānggōng,
hence the county's name.
The "Kuòdìzhì" says: Xiānglíng is thirty-five lǐ southeast of Línfén County, Jìnzhōu.
Sòng Bái says: Later Wèi called it Qínchāng County;
in the second year of Suí Dàyè, it was renamed Xiānglíng County,
because Zhào Xiāngzǐ and Jìn Xiānggōng both had tombs in this town.
1 Qín's Wèi Yāng besieged Wèi's Gùyáng
and captured it.
Wèi had Shàngjùn,
extending north to Gùyáng,
which is Gùyáng County of Hàn's Wǔyuán Commandery.
The "Kuòdìzhì" says: Gùyáng is within the borders of Yínchéng County, Yínzhōu.
According to records, Wèi built the Great Wall
from Zhèng, bordering Luò,
northward to Yínzhōu,
reaching Gùyáng County in Shèngzhōu as a fortress.
Gùyáng has continuous mountains,
extending east to the Huáng Hé,
and southwest to Xià and Huì prefectures.
Jiàng,
Hù Jiāng fān.
Xià,
Hù Yǎ fān.
2 The people of Wèi returned Hándān to Zhào.
They allied with Zhào on the Zhāngshuǐ.
The "Records of Rites: Qūlǐ" says: To approach the sacrificial animal is called "méng."
"Méng" means
to kill a sacrificial animal, smear blood,
and swear an oath to the gods.
In times of great peace,
feudal lords were not allowed to privately ally with each other.
Only when the Son of Heaven toured to the foot of the sacred mountains,
after the assembly,
would he ally with the feudal lords,
sharing likes and dislikes,
strengthening the royal house,
to show service to the gods, instruct the people, and serve the sovereign.
Whenever the state had doubts, they would form an alliance,
cursing those who were disloyal.
As for the Five Hegemons,
they would meet for affairs,
and if they disagreed, they would form an alliance.
The method of alliance
first involved digging a square pit in the ground,
killing the sacrificial animal above the pit,
cutting off the animal's left ear,
and placing it in a pearl tray;
then taking blood
and placing it in a jade vessel;
using blood for the alliance document,
and when completed,
smearing blood and reading the document.
The "Zǔo Zhuàn" says:
"The pit, the sacrificial animal, and the document are used,"
which is this.
The "History of the Former Hàn Dynasty: Monograph on Geography" says: The Turbid Zhāngshuǐ emerges from Lùgǔ Shān in Chángzǐ County, Shàngdǎng,
flows east to Yè,
and enters the Clear Zhāng.
The "Shuǐ Jīng" says: It emerges from Fājiū Shān in Chángzǐ County,
flows east to Wǔ'ān County where it meets the Clear Zhāng,
and is called Jiāozhāngkǒu.
Further east, it passes through Lièrén in Yè County,
then northeast through Jùlù and Xìndū,
and is called Héngzhāng;
then further northeast, it passes south of Píngshū County and flows east into the sea.
Zhāng,
Zhū Liáng fān.
3 Hán Zhāohóu appointed Shēn Bùhài as chancellor.
The "Shì Fǎ" says: "Zhāo" refers to having illustrious virtue and merit;
"Zhāo" refers to being sagely renowned and widely accomplished.
The "Xìng Pǔ" says: The descendants of Sìyuè were enfeoffed in Shēn.
Zhōu had Shēn Bó,
Zhèng had the grandee Shēn Hóu,
and Qí had Shēn Xiānyú.
Xiàng,
Xī Liàng fān.
Shēn Bùhài
was a humble official of Zhèng,
who studied Huáng-Lǎo and Xíngmíng,
and thus sought out Zhāohóu.
Huáng-Lǎo refers to the books of
Huángdì and Lǎozǐ.
Internally, he cultivated governance and education;
externally, he responded to the feudal lords.
For fifteen years,
until Shēnzǐ's death,
the state was well-governed and the army strong.
Shēnzǐ once asked to appoint his cousin to an official position,
but Zhāohóu did not allow it.
Shēnzǐ showed displeasure.
Zhāohóu said:
"The reason I learned from you
was to govern the state.
Now, should I grant your request and abandon your methods,
or should I implement your methods and disregard your request?
You once taught me to reward merits
and observe rank;
now you have a private request,
what should I listen to?"
Shēnzǐ then withdrew to his dwelling and asked for punishment, saying:
"Your Lord truly is such a person!"
Zhāohóu had worn-out trousers,
and ordered them to be kept.
His attendant said:
"Your Lord is not benevolent either!
You don't bestow them upon your attendants but keep them!"
Zhāohóu said:
"I have heard that an enlightened ruler values every frown and every smile.
A frown has a reason for frowning,
and a smile has a reason for smiling.
Now, trousers are surely more significant than a frown or a smile!
I must wait for someone who has rendered service."
This means that even though the trousers were worn out,
their value was still significant,
certainly more than a mere frown or smile.
However, a ruler's frowns and smiles
are of great importance.
Zhāohóu merely used this as an example.
Wéi,
Yú Wěi fān.
Pín,
same as pín,
meaning a worried, furrowed expression.
Xiào, ancient character for xiào.
1 Qín Shāng Yāng built the Jì Què palace in Xiányáng.
Suǒyǐn says: Jì Què
is the same as Wèi Què.
Éryǎ says: A guān is called a què.
Guō Pú says: They are the twin què on either side of a palace gate.
Shìmíng says: Què are on both sides of a gate,
the middle being "quē rán" (empty) as a path.
Sānfǔ Huángtú says: When a subject reaches this point,
they must reflect on what they are lacking.
Éryǎ says: A gōng is called a shì.
Guō Pú says: Gōng
refers to that which surrounds.
Shuōwén says: Tíng
is the center of the court.
Cāngjié Piān says: Tíng
means straight.
Fēngsú Tōng says: Tíng
means upright.
It refers to xiàntíng, jùntíng, and cháotíng,
all of which imply fairness and uprightness.
Sānfǔ Huángtú says: The south side of a mountain is yáng,
the north side of a river is yáng.
Since both the mountain and the river are on the yáng side,
it is called Xiányáng.
Hàn Gāodì renamed it Xīnchéng,
Wǔdì renamed it Wèichéng,
and it belonged to Yòufúfēng.
Kuòdì Zhì: The old city of Xiányáng
is fifteen lǐ east of Xiányáng Xiàn in Yōngzhōu,
and forty-five lǐ north of Cháng'ān City.
Sòng Bái says: Xiányáng Xiàn was originally the capital of Zhōu Wáng Jì,
and later Qín also made it its capital.
Sān Qín Jì: The Qín capital was south of Jiǔzōngshān,
and north of the Wèishuǐ river.
As both the mountain and the water were in yáng positions,
it was named Xiányáng.
In the twenty-ninth year,
Qín first enfeoffed Wèi Yāng in Shāng,
granting him the title of Shāng Jūn;
the historian recorded it with his later enfeoffment.
He forbade fathers, sons, and brothers from sleeping in the same room.
Xī
means to stop.
It was the custom in Qín
for fathers, sons, and brothers to live and sleep in the same room;
Shāng Jūn first changed this system
and forbade sleeping in the same room.
Yáo taught the people human relationships,
teaching them order and distinction.
Qín adopted the customs of the Xīróng,
to the extent that there was no distinction between men and women,
nor order between elders and juniors.
Shāng Jūn's current prohibition
is the ancient way,
how can it be spoken of as a mere example!
Báihǔ Tōng says: Fù (father)
means jǔ (carpenter's square),
to teach children with laws and standards.
Zǐ (son)
means zī (to multiply),
constantly and endlessly.
Xiōng (elder brother)
means kuàng (to make an analogy),
to emulate the father's laws.
Dì (younger brother)
means tì (filial piety),
to have a compliant heart and diligent conduct.
The land was gathered into a xiàn,
each xiàn had a lìng and a chéng,
totaling thirty-one xiàn.
The well-field system was abolished,
and the qiān and mò boundaries were opened up.
The Zhōulǐ says:
Six xiāng,
each xiāng having twelve thousand five hundred households.
Also, within a hundred households was called a xiāng,
five bǐ formed a xiàn,
each xiàn having two thousand five hundred households;
these were the xiàn of the six suì.
Four diàn formed a xiàn;
these were the xiàn of the zhōulǐ.
Under the Zhōu system: The Son of Heaven's domain was a thousand lǐ square,
divided into a hundred xiàn,
each xiàn having four jùn.
This is what Zhào Yāng in Zuǒzhuàn referred to as
"high-ranking officials receiving xiàn,
and low-ranking officials receiving jùn."
When Qín unified the realm,
it established thirty-six jùn
to oversee the xiàn of the realm,
and from then on, they were governed by jùn.
Shìmíng says: Xiàn
means xuán (to hang),
meaning it is "hung" from a jùn.
The Hánshū Yīnyì says:
"Large ones are called xiāng,
small ones are called jù,"
which was also a Qín system.
Guǎngyǎ says: Jù
means to gather and live together,
pronounced cǐ yù fān.
The offices of xiànlìng and xiànchéng started here.
Lìng
is pronounced lì zhèng fān.
Lìng
means to command,
to inform,
law,
regulation,
and chief;
to make one the chief of a xiàn,
to carry out commands and laws.
Chéng
means to assist,
a deputy or second-in-command.
Under the Chéng Zhōu system,
a square lǐ of land was a jǐng,
a jǐng was nine hundred mù,
and eight households each cultivated a hundred mù;
of the hundred mù in the middle,
eighty mù were public land,
and twenty mù were for dwellings.
Shǐjì Zhèngyì says: North-south paths are qiān,
east-west paths are mò.
Liú Bóchuāng says: To open up field boundary paths,
so they do not interfere with each other.
Zhǎng
is pronounced zhī liǎng fān.
2 Qín and Wèi met in Tóng.
Tóng
was the state enfeoffed to Zhōu Tóngbó,
located within the royal domain.
Shǐjì Liùguó Niánbiǎo: Shāng Jūn rebelled
and died in Tóng.
Therefore, its territory should have been within the Hàn Jīngzhào Zhèng Xiàn area.
Tóng
is pronounced tú dōng fān.
3 Zhào Chénghóu passed away.
Gōngzǐ Xiè contended with the crown prince for succession;
Xiè was defeated
and fled to Hán.
1 Qín Shāng Yāng reformed the tax laws
and implemented them.
Since the well-field system was abolished,
the Zhōu system of one-tenth was no longer used;
presumably, a tax system based on land area (mù) was established.
Gēng
is pronounced gōng héng fān.
1 Zhào Gōngzǐ Fàn attacked Hándān,
was unsuccessful, and died.
1 Qí killed its grandee, Móu.
2 Lǔ Kānggōng passed away,
and his son, Jǐnggōng Yǎn, succeeded him.
3 Wèi's title was demoted to Hóu,
submitting to the Sān Jìn.
Zhōu Chéngwáng enfeoffed Kāngshú as Wèi Hóu;
later generations advanced their title to Gōng;
now, having gradually weakened and shrunk,
their title was demoted to Hóu.
Biǎn
is pronounced bēi jiǎn fān.
1 The feudal lords met in the Jīngshī.
At that time, the world revered Zhōu,
taking Luòyáng as the Jīngshī.
Jīng

as small waters flow into it,

3 In the beginning,
Sū Qín, a man from Luòyáng, tried to persuade the King of Qín with strategies for unifying All Under Heaven,
but the King of Qín did not adopt his advice.
Sū Qín then left
and persuaded Duke Wén of Yān, saying:
“The reason Yān is not troubled by bandits and military attacks
is because Zhào acts as a screen to its south.
Moreover, when Qín attacks Yān,
the battle is fought a thousand *lǐ* away;
when Zhào attacks Yān,
the battle is fought within a hundred *lǐ*.
Yān borders Zhào to the south;
fighting within a hundred *lǐ* means it is close.
If Qín wants to attack Yān,
it must deploy troops from Pú and Tóng,
but then it would be blocked by Zhào.
Therefore, it must pass through the west of Shàngjùn,
come out from Yúnzhōng and Jiǔyuán, and only then reach Yān.
Hence, it is said that the battle is fought a thousand *lǐ* away.
There is no better plan than this.
I wish for Your Majesty to form a close alliance with Zhào;
if All Under Heaven becomes one,
then the state of Yān will certainly be without worry.”
This was Sū Qín's ultimate plan for Yān, which he had already decided in his mind.
Wéngōng followed his advice,
providing Sū Qín with carriages and horses.
He then persuaded Zhào Sùhóu, saying:
"At this present time,
among the states established east of the mountains, none is stronger than Zhào,
and what Qín fears most is also Zhào.
However, Qín dares not raise troops to attack Zhào
for fear that Hán and Wèi would assail its rear.
When Qín attacks Hán and Wèi,
there are no famous mountains or great rivers to limit its advance.
It gradually encroaches upon their territory like a silkworm devouring a leaf
until it reaches their capitals.
Hán and Wèi will be unable to withstand Qín
and will inevitably submit to Qín as its vassals.
If Qín encounters no resistance from Hán and Wèi, then disaster will fall upon Zhào.
Your servant has examined the map
of the world
and the territory of the feudal lords is five times that of Qín.
The estimated number of troops of the feudal lords is ten times that of Qín.
If the six states unite as one,
combine their strength, turn westward and attack Qín,
Qín will surely be defeated.
Those who advocate for the 'vertical alliance' (héng) all wish to carve up the territory of the feudal lords and give it to Qín.
If Qín succeeds, they themselves will become rich and honored,
while their states suffer Qín's calamities without them sharing the sorrow.
Therefore, these 'vertical alliance' proponents tirelessly use Qín's power day and night to intimidate the feudal lords
in order to gain territory.
Therefore, I wish Your Majesty would carefully consider this!
I secretly devise a plan for Your Majesty:
there is nothing better than to unite Hán, Wèi, Qí, Chǔ, Yān, and Zhào into a 'horizontal alliance' (zòngqīn) to rebel against Qín.
Let the generals and ministers of all states meet by the Huánshuǐ river,
exchange hostages, and form an alliance.
The covenant should state: 'If Qín attacks one state,
the other five states shall each send out elite troops,
either to divert Qín
or to rescue the attacked state.
If anyone fails to abide by the covenant,
the five states shall jointly attack them!'
If the feudal lords form a 'horizontal alliance' and shun Qín,
Qín's armies will surely not dare to sally forth from Hángǔ Pass to harm the states east of the mountains."
Sùhóu was greatly pleased.

is nine *lǐ* north of Fényīn County in Púzhōu,
the old city of Píshì
is one hundred eighty paces west of Lóngmén County in Jiàngzhōu.
2 King Wēi of Chǔ died.
His son King Huái Huái ascended the throne.
The *Shìfǎ* says: "One who is benevolent and merciful but dies young is called Huái;
also Huái
means 'to think'."
槐 (Huái),
read *hū guāi fān*,
also *hū guī fān*.
折 (zhé),
read *ér shè fān*.
3 Yǎn, the younger brother of Duke Tìchéng of Sòng, attacked Tìchéng;
Tìchéng fled to Qí,
and Yǎn enthroned himself as ruler.
1 Qín's Gōngzǐ Huá and Zhāng Yí led an army to besiege Púyáng in Wèi,
and took it.
The *Shǐjì Zhèngyì* says: Púyáng is in Xīchuān County of Xízhōu,

帥 (shuài),
pronounced *lǜ*.
They requested to return Púyáng to Wèi,

Yí then persuaded the King of Wèi, saying:
"Qín treats Wèi very generously,

Wèi then surrendered all fifteen counties of Shàngjùn as an apology.
Zhāng Yí returned and became prime minister of Qín.
1 Qín established Yìqú as a county,
and made its ruler a vassal.
Yìqú,
was the name of a Western Róng state,
which Qín took and made into a county.
The *Bān Zhì* says,
Yìqú Dao belongs to Běidì Commandery.
