were Qín's Běidì Commandery.
2 Qín returned Jiāo and Qǔwò to Wèi.
Having taken them, it returned them.
Qín's treatment of Wèi
was like playing with an infant in the palm of its hand.
1 Marquis Sù of Zhào died.
The *Suǒyǐn* says: Marquis Sù's personal name was Yǔ.
He established three erudite scholars (*Bówén Shī*) and three supervisors of errors (*Zuǒ, Yòu Sīguò*).
He first consulted the former lord's honored minister Féi Yì,
and increased his rank.
The *Suǒyǐn* says: King Wǔlíng's personal name was Yōng.
The *Xìngpǔ* says: The Féi surname
is descended from Féi Zǐ,
using the state as the surname.
1 Summer,
fourth month,
day *wùwǔ*,
Qín first claimed the title of king.
2 Marquis Wèi Píng (衛平侯) passed away.
His son, Sī Jūn (嗣君), ascended the throne.
Wèi (衞) had a penal slave who escaped to Wèi (魏),
and subsequently treated the illness of King Wèi (魏王)'s consort.
Sī Jūn (嗣君) heard of this,
and requested to buy him for fifty jīn (金).
Five times he tried,
but Wèi (魏) would not agree.
Then he offered Zuǒ Shì (左氏) in exchange for him.
His attendants remonstrated, saying:
"To buy one penal slave with an entire city,
is this permissible?"
Sī Jūn (嗣君) said:
"This is not what you understand!
There is no small matter in governing,
and no great matter in chaos."
King Wèi (魏王) heard of this and said:
"When a ruler has a desire,
not to listen is inauspicious."
So he loaded him into a carriage and sent him,
presenting him simply.
This is merely a statement made by followers of Shēn (申) and Hán (韓).
1 Qín (秦)'s Zhāng Yí (張儀) led an army to attack Wèi (魏),
and took Shǎn (陝).
The Bān Zhì (班志) states: Shǎn (陝) county belonged to Hóngnóng Jùn (弘農郡),
formerly the state of Guó (虢).
Běi Guó (北虢) was in Dàyáng (大陽),
Dōng Guó (東虢) in Xíngyáng (滎陽),
and Xī Guó (西虢) in Yōng Zhōu (雍州).
Zhōu (周) and Shào (召) divided Shǎn (陝) to govern,
which is this Shǎnxī (陝西).
Shuài (帥),
pronounced as lǜ (率).
Shǎn (陝),
pronounced shǎn.
Shào (召),
pronounced as Shào (邵).
2 Sū Qín (蘇秦) had an affair with the夫人 (fūrén) of Yān Wén Gōng (燕文公).
Yì Wáng (易王) found out about it.
Sū Qín (蘇秦), fearful,
then persuaded Yì Wáng (易王) saying:
"If I stay in Yān (燕), I cannot make Yān (燕) strong,
but if I am in Qí (齊), then Yān (燕) will be strong."
Yì Wáng (易王) agreed to this.
So Sū Qín (蘇秦) feigned having offended Yān (燕) and fled to Qí (齊),
where Qí Xuān Wáng (齊宣王) made him a guest minister.
Sū Qín (蘇秦) advised King Qí (齊王) to build high palaces
and large park-like gardens,
to demonstrate his contentment,
hoping to weaken Qí (齊) for the benefit of Yān (燕).
1 Qín (秦)'s Zhāng Yí (張儀) and the prime ministers of Qí (齊) and Chǔ (楚) met at Niè Sāng (齧桑).
2 Both Hán (韓) and Yān (燕) claimed kingship.
Zhào Wǔlíng Wáng (趙武靈王) alone refused,
saying:
"Without the reality,
how dare I assume the title?"
He ordered the people of his state to call him Jūn (君).
Zhào Wǔlíng Wáng (趙武靈王)'s refusal to claim kingship
was not about maintaining the distinction between ruler and subject,
nor was it out of humility,
but rather because he sought a greater desire which his strength was not yet able to fulfill to his satisfaction.
Chǔ (處),
pronounced chǔ.
Lìng (令),
pronounced lìng,
meaning "to cause";
also pronounced lìng,
meaning "command."
Fēn (分),
pronounced fèn.
Chèn (稱),
pronounced chēng.
1 Qín (秦)'s Zhāng Yí (張儀) returned from Niè Sāng (齧桑) and was dismissed from his post as prime minister.
He became prime minister of Wèi (魏),
intending to make Wèi (魏) serve Qín (秦) first, and then the other feudal lords would follow suit;
but King Wèi (魏王) did not listen.
King Qín (秦王) attacked Wèi (魏),
taking Qǔwò (曲沃) and Píngzhōu (平周),
and secretly favored Zhāng Yí (張儀) even more.
1 The king passed away,
and his son, Shènjìng Wáng (慎靚王), was established.
2 Yān Yì Wáng (燕易王) passed away,
and his son Kuài (噲) ascended the throne.
3 King Qí (齊王) enfeoffed Tián Yīng (田嬰) in Xuē (薛).
The Bān Zhì (班志) states: Xuē (薛) county belonged to the state of Lǔ (魯),
formerly the state of Xi Hēizhòng (夏奚仲);
later it moved to Pī (邳),
where Zhòng Huǐ (仲虺) resided.
The Kuòdì Zhì (括地志) states: The old city of Xuē (薛) is within the present-day Téng Xiàn (滕縣) boundary of Xú Zhōu (徐州).
The Shǐjì Zhèngyì (史記正義) says: The old city of Xuē (薛) is forty-four lǐ (里) south of present-day Téng Xiàn (滕縣) in Xú Zhōu (徐州).
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: During the Warring States period,
and between Qín (秦) and Xiàng (項),
those who were powerfully appointed or given additional enfeoffed territories
generally assumed their titles,
or simply received their noble ranks,
such as Jìngguō (靖郭) and Wǔ'ān (武安).
This became even more common in the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
being an additional honorific title beyond the standard enfeoffment.
The Shǐjì Lièzhuàn (史記列傳) says: Yīng (嬰)'s posthumous title was Jìngguō Jūn (靖郭君).
The Suǒyǐn (索隱) says: Jìngguō (靖郭)
was either a title or a fief name,
hence Sī Jūn (駟鈞) of Hàn (漢) was enfeoffed as Jìngguō Hóu (靖郭侯).
"The accounts of the five officials
must be listened to daily and reviewed frequently."
The Jì Zēngzǐ Wèn (記曾子問) states: When a feudal lord departs,
he appoints the five officials of the state before leaving.
The commentary says: The five officials
are the five grand masters who manage affairs.
To appoint them means
to instruct them in their duties.
The Zhèngyì (正義) says: Based on the Zhí Tàizǎi (職太宰), it states: "establish his shepherds,
set up his overseers,
appoint his advisors,
and empower his five (officials)."
This indicates that feudal lords had three ministers and five grand masters.
The classic text mentions "five officials,"
thus referring to the five grand masters.
As for the subordinate grand masters,
their number was great,
and saying "five" simply
refers to those who managed state affairs.
Not mentioning the appointment of ministers
is because they either accompanied the ruler,
or remained in the state as guardians,
generally presiding over all officials,
like the Three Dukes,
not specifically managing one matter,
and also out of respect for them.
Since the five grand masters were appointed,
it is understood that ministers were also appointed,
hence it is not explicitly stated that ministers were appointed.
I believe that these "five officials"
also refer to the five grand masters who manage affairs.
Shù (數),
pronounced shuò.
Later, being weary of it,
he entrusted everything to Jìngguō Jūn (靖郭君).
Jìngguō Jūn (靖郭君) thereby gained sole authority over Qí (齊).
Jìngguō Jūn (靖郭君) wanted to fortify Xuē (薛).
A guest said to Jìngguō Jūn (靖郭君):
"Have you not heard of the great fish in the sea?
Nets cannot stop it,
hooks cannot catch it.
But if it thrashes and loses water,
then ants will control it.
Now, Qí (齊),
is also your water.
If you long possess Qí (齊),
what need is there for Xuē (薛)?
If you should lose Qí (齊),
even if the city walls of Xuē (薛) reached to the sky,
what good would it be to rely on it?"
So he did not proceed with fortifying the city.
Lóng (隆),
meaning high,
and exalted.
Yōng (庸),
meaning ordinary.
Jìngguō Jūn (靖郭君) had forty
sons,
of whom the son by a lowly concubine was named Wén (文).
Wén (文) was astute and resourceful,
Tōng (通) means intelligent.
Tǎng (儻) means extraordinary and outstanding.
Ráo Zhìlüè (饒智略) means having abundant wisdom and strategies.
Jìngguō Jūn (靖郭君) made Wén (文) manage the household and entertain guests.
The guests competed to praise his merits,
and all requested Jìngguō Jūn (靖郭君) to make Wén (文) his heir.
When Jìngguō Jūn (靖郭君) died,
Wén (文) succeeded him as Duke Xuē (薛公),
and was known as Mèngcháng Jūn (孟嘗君).
The Shǐjì Lièzhuàn (史記列傳) says: his posthumous title was Mèngcháng Jūn (孟嘗君).
The Suǒyǐn (索隱) says: He was known as Mèngcháng Jūn (孟嘗君);
to say it was a posthumous title
is incorrect.
Mèng (孟) was his courtesy name;
Cháng (嘗) was the name of his fief.
Cháng (嘗) fief was adjacent to Xuē (薛).
He provided them with residences and generous treatment,
Shě Yè (舍業) means building residences and establishing livelihoods for them.
He always had several thousand retainers,
each believing that Mèngcháng Jūn (孟嘗君) was close to him,
and thus Mèngcháng Jūn (孟嘗君)'s fame spread throughout the world.
Chén Guāng 曰: A jūnzi raises shǐ
for the sake of the people.
The Yì says:
"The shèngrén nourishes the xián
and extends it to all people."
This is from the tuàn cí of the Yí guà.
The character "為" (wéi),
pronounced yú wěi.
Their virtue is sufficient to strengthen transformation and rectify customs;
their talent is sufficient to put the political framework in order and restore discipline.
Dùn (頓),
means to rectify.
Fú (夫),
pronounced fú.
Their strength is sufficient to solidify benevolence and reinforce righteousness.
Greatly, they benefit all under heaven;
in a small way, they benefit a single state.
Therefore, the jūnzi bestows generous stipends to enrich them
and elevates their ranks to honor them.
To raise one person and benefit ten thousand
is the way of nurturing the xián.
Now, Mèngcháng Jūn's way of raising shǐ
disregards intelligence or foolishness,
and does not distinguish between good and bad.
He steals his ruler's emoluments
to establish private cliques,
creates false reputations,
upwards to insult his ruler,
downwards to harm his people.
This is a chief among treacherous men.
How can such a person be esteemed?
The Shū says:
"Shòu became the lord of fugitives and a gathering place for them throughout the world."
This is what it means.
4 Mèngcháng Jūn was invited to Chǔ,
and the King of Chǔ presented him with an xiàngchuáng.
Dēngtú Zhí personally delivered it.
Xiàngchuáng (象牀)
is made of elephant tusks.
Dēngtú (登徒)
is the surname;
Zhí (直)
is his given name.
Yí (遺),
pronounced yú jì.
He said to Gōngsūn Xù, a retainer of Mèngcháng Jūn:
"The xiàngchuáng is worth a thousand jīn.
If it is damaged even by a hair,
selling one's wife and children would not be enough to compensate.
If you can prevent me from making this trip,
I have an ancestral treasured sword,
which I am willing to present to you."
Gōngsūn Xù agreed.
The Xìngpǔ says: The Gōngsūn clan originated from Huángdì.
The Shìmíng says: Jiàn (劍)
means jiǎn (檢),
that by which extraordinary situations are prevented and controlled.
Xù (戌),
pronounced xù.
Cháng (償),
pronounced chén yáng,
meaning to repay.
Nuò (諾),
pronounced nú gè.
To agree to someone verbally is called nuò.
"The reason why all small states present their prime ministerial seals to you, my lord,
is because you are able to raise the poor
and preserve the dying and restore the cut-off.
Therefore, none do not rejoice in your righteousness
and admire your integrity.
Now, you have just arrived in Chǔ and accepted an xiàngchuáng.
What will the states you have not yet visited think of you?"
Mèngcháng Jūn said:
"Good."
So he did not accept it.
Gōngsūn Xù hurried away.
Before he reached the inner chambers,
Mèngcháng Jūn called him back,
and said:
"Why is your step so high,
and your spirit so uplifted?"
Gōngsūn Xù answered truthfully.
Mèngcháng Jūn then wrote on his door plaque:
"Anyone who can glorify Wén's name,
stop Wén's faults,
or privately acquire treasures from outside,
should promptly enter and remonstrate!"
Chén Guāng 曰: Mèngcháng Jūn can be said to be skilled in accepting remonstrance.
If the words are good,
even if they harbor deceptive intentions,
he will still use them,
let alone those who serve their superiors with utmost loyalty and no self-interest!
The Shī says:
"Gather fú and gather fěi,
do not discard the lower part."
This is from the Gǔfēng of Shī Bèibù.
Máo Shì Zhuàn says: Fēng (葑),
is xū (須).
Fěi (菲),
is wù (芴).
Zhèng Shì Jiān says: These two vegetables,
are like turnip and fú (葍).
Both the upper and lower parts are edible.
However, their roots sometimes taste good
and sometimes bad.
Those who gather them should not discard their leaves just because the roots are bad.
Xiàtǐ (下體)
refers to the roots and stems.
Lù Jī Cǎomù Shū says: Fēng (葑),
is wújīng (蕪菁).
Guō Pú says: It is today's sōngcài (菘菜).
Lù Démíng says: Jiāngnán has sōng (菘),
Jiāngběi has mánjīng (蔓菁).
They are similar but different.
The Ěryǎ says: Fěi (菲),
is wù (芴);
it also says: Fěi (菲),
is xīcài (息菜).
Guō Pú says: Fěi (菲),
wù (芴),
is tǔguā (土瓜);
xīcài (息菜),
resembles wújīng (蕪菁),
with purplish-red flowers,
edible.
Fú (葍),
has large leaves,
white flowers,
roots like fingers,
white in color,
edible.
Fěi (菲),
pronounced fū wěi.
Bèibù (邶),
pronounced pú mèi.
Wù (芴),
pronounced fú fú.
Màn (蔓),
pronounced mó guān.
Fú (葍),
pronounced fāng liù.
5 Hán Xuānhuì Wáng wanted to appoint Gōng Zhòng and Gōng Shú to govern simultaneously.
He asked Miù Liú.
He replied:
"It is not permissible.
Jìn employed six qīng and the state was divided;
Qí Jiǎn Gōng employed Chén Chéngzǐ and Kàn Zhǐ and was killed;
Wèi employed Xīshǒu and Zhāng Yí and the land west of the Hé was lost.
The six qīng of Jìn were
the Zhì, Fàn, Zhōngháng, Zhào, Hán, and Wèi clans.
Since Jìn Wén Gōng and Xiāng Gōng,
they successively held state power,
and later all grew powerful,
eventually dividing the state of Jìn.
Qí Jiǎn Gōng made Kàn Zhǐ regent,
and Chén Chéngzǐ feared him.
Later, the Chén clan killed Kàn Zhǐ
and assassinated Jiǎn Gōng.
Kàn (闞),
is a surname derived from a city.
Sū Dài said: If Xīshǒu is the Wèi prime minister,
he will certainly favor Hán and slight Wèi;
if Zhāng Yí is the prime minister,
he will certainly favor Qín and slight Wèi.
When two prime ministers each rely on allied states for influence externally and contend for power internally,
Wèi will inevitably shrink day by day.
Kàn (闞),
pronounced hù jiān.
Háng (行),
pronounced hù gāng.
Héng (恆),
pronounced hù dēng.
Zú (卒),
pronounced zǐ xù.
Xiàng (相),
pronounced xì liàng.
The more powerful one will establish factions internally;
the less powerful one will rely on external influence.
If your treacherous officials establish internal factions to become arrogant towards their lord,
and form external alliances to encroach upon territory,
your state will be in danger."

Shènjìng Wáng
(諱 Dìng) was the son of Xiǎn Wáng.
This is a compound posthumous title.
According to the method of posthumous titles,
the rules for posthumous titles say:
"Agile and respectful is called Shèn (慎);
gentle in virtue and bringing peace to the multitude is called Jìng (靖)."
Jìng (靚),
pronounced jí zhèng.
1 Wèi further demoted its title to Jūn.
In the 23rd year of Xiǎn Wáng,
Wèi had already been demoted to Hóu;
caught between Qín and Wèi,
its state grew weaker day by day,
and so its title was further demoted to Jūn.
更,
Jū Mèng fān.
貶,
Bēi Jiǎn fān.
1 Qín attacked Hán,
and took Yān.
In the Chūnqiū it says,
“Jìn defeated the Chǔ army at Yānlíng,”
which is this Yān.
Bān Zhì writes it as
“Yānlíng,”
belonging to Yǐngchuān Jùn.
鄢,
sound Yè Wǎn fān,
also Yú Jiàn fān;
Shīgǔ pronounced it Yǎn.
Shǐjì Zhèngyì says: Fifteen lǐ northwest of Yānlíng Xiàn, Xǔzhōu, there is the ancient city of Yānlíng.
2 Wèi Huì Wáng passed away,
and his son Xiāng Wáng was enthroned.
Suǒyǐn says: The Xìběn states: Xiāng Wáng's
name was Sì.
Now, upon examination, Xìběn is in fact Shìběn;
Sīmǎ Zhēn avoided the Tang taboo
and changed
“Shì”
to
“Xì”.
Kǎoyì says: The Shǐjì Wèi Shìjiā says: Huì Wáng died in his 36th year,
and his son Xiāng Wáng was enthroned.
Xiāng Wáng died in his 16th year,
and his son Āi Wáng was enthroned.
Āi Wáng died in his 23rd year,
and his son Zhāo Wáng was enthroned.
The Liùguó Biǎo shows Huì Wáng's first year as Xīnhài,
ending in Bǐngxū;
Xiāng Wáng's first year as Dīnghài,
ending in Rényín;
Āi Wáng's first year as Guǐmǎo,
ending in Yǐchǒu.
According to Dù Yù's Chūnqiū Hòuxù, in the early Tàikāng period,
someone in Jí Xiàn unearthed an old tomb,
and found many ancient books.
Its Jìnián Piān began from Xià, Yīn, and Zhōu,
all about the royal affairs of the Three Dynasties,
without distinguishing between various states;
it only specifically recorded the affairs of the state of Jìn,
starting from Shāng Shú,
then Wén Hóu, Zhāo Hóu,
down to Qúwò Zhuāng Bó,
all using the Xià calendar,
with events arranged chronologically;
when Jìn was destroyed,
it only recorded Wèi's affairs,
down to the 20th year of Wèi Āi Wáng: this was probably the historical record of the state of Wèi.
Āi Wáng, in the Shǐjì,
is the son of Xiāng Wáng, and grandson of Huì Wáng.
The ancient book Jìnián Piān states that Huì Wáng changed his reign title in his 36th year,
starting from year one,
and died in the 16th year after the change of reign title,
who is Huì Wáng;
it is suspected that the Shǐjì mistakenly divided Huì Chéng's reign into a later king's years.
Āi Wáng only died in his 23rd year,
hence he was not given a posthumous title,
but was called
“Jīn Wáng”.
Péi Yīn's commentary on Wèi Shìjiā quotes Hé Qiáo saying: The Jìnián starts from Huángdì,
and ends with the Jīn Wáng of Wèi;
Jīn Wáng is
the son of Wèi Huì Chéng Wáng.
According to Tàishǐ Gōng's book,
Huì Chéng Wáng is simply referred to as Huì Wáng;
Huì Wáng's son is called Xiāng Wáng,
and Xiāng Wáng's son is called Āi Wáng.
Huì Wáng died in his 36th year,
Xiāng Wáng was enthroned and died in his 16th year,
making a total of 52 years for Huì and Xiāng.
Now, according to the ancient text, Huì Chéng Wáng was enthroned for 36 years,
changed his reign title,
called it year one,
and died in the 17th year after the change of reign title.
Tàishǐ Gōng's book mistakenly divided Huì Chéng's reign into the years of two kings.
The Shìběn states that Huì Wáng begot Xiāng Wáng but no Āi Wáng;
therefore
“Jīn Wáng”
is Wèi Xiāng Wáng.
Since that was Wèi's history,
the Wèi affairs recorded must be true,
so we follow it now.
Someone said:
“Looking at him, he does not resemble a ruler;
approaching him, one feels no awe.
Suddenly he asked: 'How can the world be settled?'
I replied: 'It will be settled by unification.'
'Who can unify it?'”
This sentence
was Wèi Xiāng Wáng asking Mèngzǐ.
“'Who can bestow it?'”
This sentence was also asked by Xiāng Wáng.
“'Does the king know about the sprouts?
If there is a drought between the seventh and eighth months,

Suǒyǐn (索隱) states: King Wǔ (武王)
was named Dàng (蕩).
He did not favor Zhāng Yí (張儀);
and upon his ascension,
many of his sycophantic ministers slandered and disparaged him.
"Huǐduǎn" (毀短) means
to slander and point out his shortcomings.
They all abandoned the "Héng" (衡) (Alliance),
and rejoined the "Zòng" (從) (Alliance).
Zhāng Yí (張儀) persuaded King Wǔ of Qín (秦武王), saying:
"For Your Majesty's sake,
if there is a change in the east,
Hán (韓) and Wèi (魏) are both to the east of Qín (秦).
"Shuō" (說)
is pronounced "shì ruì" (式芮).
Your servant hears that the King of Qí (齊王) deeply detests your servant;
wherever your servant is,
Qí (齊) will surely attack it.
Your servant wishes to offer his unworthy self to go to Liáng (梁),
"bùxiào" (不肖)
is a humble expression meaning 'having no resemblance' [to worthiness].
Wèi's (魏) capital was Dàliáng (大梁).
Qí (齊) and Liáng (梁) will engage in battle and be unable to disengage,
meaning their armies will be locked in battle,
each wishing to withdraw but unable to do so.
[Qín (秦) can then] enter Sānchuān (三川),
seize the Son of Heaven,
and review the maps and registers;
this is the foundation of a royal enterprise!"
Zhāng Yí (張儀) wished to undermine Zhōu (周) for Qín (秦),
and always made this the main point of his persuasion.
"Xiá" (挾)
is pronounced "hù jiá" (戶頰).
The King of Qí (齊王) indeed attacked Liáng (梁),
and the King of Liáng (梁王) was afraid.
Zhāng Yí (張儀) said:
"Your Majesty need not worry!"
Meaning, "do not take it as a worry."
He then sent his retainer to Chǔ (楚),
asking him to tell the King of Qí (齊王):
"Zhī" (之)
means "to go,"
or "to arrive."
[Zhāng Yí (張儀)] dared not directly send an envoy to Qí (齊),

"How deeply Your Majesty trusts Yí (儀) to Qín (秦)!"

"For what reason?"

Now Your Majesty indeed attacks Liáng (梁);
this means Your Majesty depletes your country internally and attacks an allied country externally,
and moreover gives credence to Yí (儀) in the eyes of the King of Qín (秦王)."
The King of Qí (齊王) then withdrew his troops and returned.
Zhāng Yí (張儀) served as chancellor of Wèi (魏) for one year,

Yí (儀) and Sū Qín (蘇秦) both traveled among the feudal lords with the arts of "Zònghéng" (縱橫),

There was also Gōngsūn Yǎn (公孫衍) of Wèi (魏),

The others, such as Sū Dài (蘇代), Sū Lì (蘇厲), Zhōu Zuì (周最), Lóu Huǎn (樓緩), and their like,

all vying with each other in sophistry and deceit,

The Xìngpǔ (姓譜) states: The Zhōu (周) surname originated from the son of King Píng of Zhōu (周平王),

Wēngōng (溫公) said: "Upon examining the years and events, they do not match.

"Yí (儀) and Qín (秦) would be ashamed of it."

Comets are what the world calls "broom stars,"

They also said: Bó stars are a type of comet;

Bó means "to be violent,"

and its disaster is more severe than a huì.
Astronomical texts state that the essences of the five planets become ominous phenomena;

A county magistrate had unfurled his bedding and his mat was worn out;
Wèi Sìjūn heard of it
and bestowed a new mat upon him.
The magistrate was greatly astonished,
believing the lord to be divine.
He also sent someone to pass through a frontier pass and market,
bribing him with gold.
This was likely bribing the official in charge of the pass and market.
The Zhōu Lǐ states: The Sīguān manages the regulations for national goods,
to connect gateways and markets;
the official who controls the entry and exit of goods and bribes
manages their prohibitions and their taxes.
The Sīshì manages the governance, education, policies, and penalties of the market,
as well as weights, measures, and prohibitions.
During the Warring States period,
these were combined into one office.
量 (liàng),
sound liàng.
He asked if a guest passing through had given him gold,
and if he had sent it back;
"sent back" (回遣)
means returning the gold.
He also loved Xiè Jī,
and esteemed Rú'ěr,
but feared that their love and esteem would cause them to obstruct him.
泄 (Xiè),
a surname;
it is the same as 洩.
During the Chūnqiū period, Zhèng had a Grand Master named Xiè Jià,
and Chén had a Grand Master named Xiè Yě.
如 (Rú)
is also a surname.
Zhāng Shǒujié mistakenly believed Rú'ěr to be the name of a Grand Master of Wèi;
this is incorrect,
he was probably a Grand Master of Wèi.
At that time, King Wèi had a concubine named Rú Jī.
重 (zhòng),
sound zhòng (as in "heavy" or "important").
薄 (Bó),
a surname.
Fēngsú Tōng states:
Bó Yí was a worthy man from Wèi.
敵 (dí),
means "to match".
偶 (ǒu),
means "a pair," "a counterpart."
"using these to compare one another."
參 (cēn),
means "three";
to be arranged side by side,
to be interspersed.
Xúnzǐ discussed this, saying: Marquis Chéng and Sìjūn
were rulers who accumulated wealth and calculated carefully,
but they had not yet achieved gaining the people.
Zǐchǎn
was one who gained the people,
but had not yet achieved good governance.
Guǎn Zhòng
was one who achieved good governance,
but had not yet achieved cultivating rites.
Therefore, those who cultivate rites become kings,
those who achieve good governance become strong,
those who gain the people become secure,
and those who merely accumulate wealth perish.
1 Qín attacked Zhào,
seizing two cities.
1 Qín attacked Zhào,
seizing Shíchéng.
Shǐjì Zhèngyì states: In the Dìlǐ Zhì,
Yòu Běipíng has Shíchéng County.
Kuòdì Zhì: Shíchéng is ninety *lǐ* southwest of Línlǜ County in Xiāng Zhōu.
It is likely the Shíchéng in Xiāng Zhōu.
I (the commentator) say that Shíchéng in Běipíng
is in Yān territory,
and Shíchéng in Xiāng Zhōu
is in Wèi territory;
neither is Zhào territory.
This Shíchéng is the city of Líshí County in Hàn's Xīhé;
the Tuòbá Wèi divided Xīhé,
established Wǔchéng Commandery,
and also established Shíchéng County.
This is probably that place.
相 (xiàng),
sound xìliàng fān.
慮 (lǜ),
sound lú.
燕 (Yān),
sound yīnjiān fān.
2 Marquis Ráng of Qín again became Chancellor.
3 Chǔ wanted to attack Qí and Hán jointly with Qín,
and then intended to seize Zhōu.
The King sent Dōngzhōu Wǔgōng to tell the Chǔ Lìngyǐn Zhāozǐ:
"Zhōu cannot be seized."
The Lìngyǐn
was Chǔ’s chief minister,
holding the reins of the state’s government,
similar to Qín’s prime minister.
Lìng,
pronounced lì zhèng.
"If you intend to seize Zhōu, there is nothing there;
even so,
why can it not be seized?"
Wǔgōng said:
"The land of Xīzhōu,
if we combine the long and shorten the short,
is no more than a hundred *lǐ*.
It is nominally the common lord of all under Heaven,"
meaning that all under Heaven jointly honored Zhōu as the lord of the feudal lords.
Dù Yòu said: Luòyáng
was the land of ancient Chéngzhōu.
The old city thirty *lǐ* east of present-day Luòyáng,
was Zhōu’s secondary capital.
Jìn led the feudal lords to build its walls,
for King Jìng to reside in.
During King Xiào’s reign, his younger brother Huán Gōng was enfeoffed in Hénán to continue the official duties of the Duke of Zhōu;
his grandson, Huì Gōng, then enfeoffed his youngest son in Gǒng,
named Dōngzhōu.
When King Nǎn ascended the throne,
Dōngzhōu and Xīzhōu were administered separately,
and the capital was moved to Xīzhōu,
which was the royal city.
Shuài,
read as *shuài*.
Shǎo,
pronounced shǐ zhào.
Gǒng,
pronounced jū yǒng.
Nǎn,
pronounced nú bǎn.
"Acquiring its populace is not enough to strengthen the military.
Even so,
those who attack it will be called regicides.
Yet, there are still those who wish to attack it,
because the sacrificial vessels are there."
This refers to the sacrificial vessels passed down from the Three Dynasties,
such as the Nine Tripods.
"People still attack it;
if a deer in a marsh were to put on a tiger’s skin,
people would attack it ten thousand times more fiercely.
Splitting Chǔ’s land
is enough to enrich one’s state;
diminishing Chǔ’s reputation
is enough to honor the King.
Now, you wish to destroy the common lord of all under Heaven
and appropriate the vessels passed down from the Three Dynasties.
If the vessels go south,
then troops will arrive!"
Thereupon, Chǔ’s plan was halted and not carried out.
1 Qín’s Bái Qǐ defeated the Zhào army,
beheading twenty thousand,
and took Guānglángchéng.
Suǒyǐn says: Geographical records do not mention Guānglángchéng,
it probably belonged to the state of Zhào.
Shǐjì Zhèngyì says: The old city of Guāngláng
is twenty *lǐ* west of Gāopíng Xiàn in Zézhōu.
Kāng says: Originally Zhōngshān territory,
Zhào Wǔlíng Wáng took it,
and its land was in Dài.
I examined the history, where Dài and Guānglángchéng are written together,
so Kāng’s idea that its land was in Dài is acceptable.
It also says it was originally Zhōngshān territory;
Zhōngshān and Dài were formerly two separate states,
Dài was on the north side of the mountains,
Zhōngshān on the south side;
since it says it was in Dài,
it should not also say it was originally Zhōngshān territory.
According to Kāng’s view,
he perhaps thought that Guāngláng was originally Dài territory,
and after Zhào Xiāngzǐ destroyed Dài, Zhōngshān encroached upon and occupied Guāngláng territory;
after Wǔlíng Wáng destroyed Zhōngshān,
he then acquired the land of Guāngláng.
Bái Qǐ deployed troops from Shàngjùn, Jiǔyuán, and Yúnzhōng,
and was then able to defeat the Zhào army
and take Guāngláng.
Since the history does not first describe the route of his military campaign,
and there is no later examination,
the location of Guānglángchéng
can be left as doubtful.
West of Qīan Xiàn in Fúfēng there is a great Lǒngshān,
named Lǒngdǐ,
traversing which takes seven days for those going up.
From Lǒng westward,
it was originally the land of the Jìróng, Qíróng, Dī, and Qiāng;
Qín pushed back and expanded for generations,
establishing Lǒngxī Jùn on that land.
Cuò,
pronounced qī gè,
also cāng gù.
Qīan,
pronounced kǔ jiān.
Qí,
pronounced hù guān.
He captured it.
According to records, the Qín army at that time used the route from Bājùn Zhǐ Xiàn through Shǔ to attack and capture Chǔ’s Qiánzhōng.
Qián,
pronounced *qín*.
Hǎnběi refers to the lands of Wǎn, Yè, Fán, Dèng, Suí, Táng north of the Hàn River.
Shàngyōng
was Cáo Wèi’s Xīnchéng,
and Táng’s Fánglíng Jùn territory.
1 Qín’s Bái Qǐ attacked Chǔ,
taking Yān, Dèng, and Xīlíng.
Shǐjì Zhèngyì says: Yān and Dèng are both in Xiāngzhōu.
Kuòdì Zhì: The old city of Yān is three *lǐ* north of Ānyǎng in Xiāngzhōu,
the state of ancient Yānzǐ.
Also, according to Shuǐjīng Zhù,
Yānchéng should be south of Yíchéng,
where the Yān River is.
Zuǒzhuàn: Chǔ’s Qū Xiá attacked Luó and Yān,
crossing in disorder,
which is that place.
Xú Guǎng says: Xīlíng belongs to Jiāngxià.
I believe Xīlíng is Yílíng.
Bān Zhì: Yílíng Xiàn belonged to Nánjùn.
Shuǐjīng: The Jiāng River flows east past Yílíng Xiàn,
and then east past Xīlíng Gorge;
presumably the county seat is not far from the gorge.
Xià,
pronounced hù yǎ.
2 The King of Qín sent an envoy to inform the King of Zhào,
wishing to hold a friendly meeting at Héwài Mǐnchí.
The King of Zhào wished not to go,
but Lián Pō and Lìn Xiāngrú advised:
Xìng Pǔ: The surname Lián
is descended from Zhuāndì’s great-grandson Dàlián.
Pō,
pronounced pǔ hé.
"If the King does not go,
it will show Zhào to be weak and timid."
So the King of Zhào went,
and Xiāngrú accompanied him.
Lián Pō escorted him to the border,
and took leave of the King,
saying:
"The King’s journey,
judging by the distance and the conclusion of the meeting rituals,
will take no more than thirty days for his return;
if he does not return in thirty days,
then please establish the crown prince to cut off Qín’s hopes."
The King agreed to this.
They met at Miǎnchí.
The King drank with King Zhào,
this sentence should read
"King Qín drank with King Zhào",
then the meaning will be clear.
King Qín requested King Zhào to play the *sè*,
the *sè* has twenty-five strings,
made by Fúxī.
The *Shǐjì* says: The Qín Emperor ordered Sùnǚ to play the fifty-string *sè*;
the Emperor's sorrow would not cease,
so he broke its *sè* into twenty-five strings.
The people of Zhào were skilled at the *sè*,
so Qín requested him to play it.
*Sè*,
pronounced `sè` (色櫛翻).
Lìn Xiāngrú in turn requested King Qín to play the *fǒu*,
the *fǒu*
is a pottery vessel.
The *Ěryǎ* says: An *àng* is called a *fǒu*;
the commentary says: It is a basin.
Yáng Yùn said:
"Looking up at the sky, striking the *fǒu* and singing 'wūwū',
that is Qín music."
The *Shuōwén* says: The *fǒu* is used to hold wine;
the people of Qín played it to mark time for music.
Liú Xǔ said: The *fǒu* is like a foot basin,
it was an instrument of the ancient Xīróng;
the Qín custom consequently adopted its use.
Its shape is like an overturned basin,
and it is struck with four sticks.
復 (fù),
pronounced `fù` (扶又翻),
also sounds like its character.
缶 (fǒu),
pronounced `fǒu` (方九翻).
惲 (Yùn),
pronounced `Yùn` (於粉翻).
盛 (shèng),
pronounced `shèng` (時征翻).
昫 (Xǔ),
pronounced `Xǔ` (旴句翻).
Xiāngrú said:
"Within five paces,
I request to be allowed to splash Your Majesty with my neck's blood!"
Meaning he would kill King Qín.
頸 (jǐng),
pronounced `jǐng` (居郢翻).
濺 (jiàn),
pronounced `jiàn` (音箭),
Kāng's pronunciation is `zàn` (康音贊),
meaning to stain and sprinkle.
汙 (wū),
pronounced `wū` (烏故翻).
Xiāngrú glared and shouted at him,
and all his attendants cowered.
靡 (mí)
means the appearance of being dispirited and listless.
Also means displeased.
When the feast concluded,
Qín ultimately could not impose anything on Zhào;
the people of Zhào had also made extensive preparations for it,
so Qín dared not make a move.
King Zhào returned to his state,
and appointed Lìn Xiāngrú as Grand Councilor,
his rank above Lián Pō.
Lián Pō said:
"I am a general of Zhào,
with merits in attacking cities and fighting in the field.
Lìn Xiāngrú was always a lowly person,
merely by his eloquence his rank is above mine.
I am ashamed,
and cannot bear to be below him!"
He publicly declared:
"If I see Xiāngrú,
I will surely humiliate him!"
'To publicly declare' means
to announce one's words to the outside (publicly).
He was unwilling to attend meetings;
at every court audience,
he often claimed illness,
not wishing to contend for rank.
When he went out and saw him from afar,
he would invariably pull his carriage away and hide to avoid him.
*Nì*
means to hide,
or to conceal.
Xiāngrú said:
"Compared to King Qín, how do you regard General Lián?"
(His attendant) replied:
"Not as good."
*Ruò*
means like or comparable.
"Now, with the might of King Qín, yet I, Xiāngrú, dared to shout at him in court,
humiliating his ministers;
this refers to the time I requested King Qín to play the *fǒu*.
Would I only fear General Lián?!"
"But I reflect on this:
The reason why mighty Qín
dares not deploy troops against Zhào
is merely because the two of us are here.
Now if two tigers fight together,
their situation is such that both cannot survive.
The reason I do this
is to prioritize the urgent matters of the state before my personal grudges!"
Lián Pō heard this,
bared his upper body, carried a thorn branch, and arrived at Lìn Xiāngrú's gate to apologize.
A *jīng*
is used for flogging,
so he carried it to ask for punishment.
'Bared upper body' means
baring and exposing one's flesh.
笞 (chī),
pronounced `chī` (丑之翻).
3 Initially,
the Yān people attacked Ānpíng.
Tián Dān, a market official of Línzī, was in Ānpíng.
He had all his kinsmen reinforce the axles of their chariots with iron cages.
When the city fell,
people rushed out through the gate,
but their chariots broke down due to fractured axles,
and they were captured by Yān.
Only Tián Dān's kinsmen, with their iron-reinforced axles, managed to escape
and fled to Jìmò.
At this time, all of Qí territory belonged to Yān,
with only Jǔ and Jìmò remaining uncaptured.
Yuè Yì then combined the Right Army and the Vanguard to besiege Jǔ,
and the Left Army and the Rearguard to besiege Jìmò.
The Grand Administrator of Jìmò went out to battle and died.
The people of Jìmò said:
"In the battle of Ānpíng,
Tián Dān's kinsmen were saved by their iron-reinforced axles.
This shows he is very resourceful and skilled in military affairs."
So they jointly appointed him as general to resist Yān.
Yuè Yì besieged the two cities,
but could not overcome them for a full year.
He then ordered the lifting of the siege,
with each army withdrawing nine *lǐ* from the city to build encampments,
issuing an order:
"Do not capture any citizens who come out of the city;
provide relief to those in distress
and allow them to return to their former occupations."
*Jí*
means 'to approach' or 'to return to'.
Fearing that the new populace might think of Qí and rebel,
he used this to pacify them.
Someone then slandered him to Yān Zhāo Wáng, saying:
"Yuè Yì's wisdom and strategy surpass others.
In his campaign against Qí,
he captured over seventy cities in an instant.
Now only two cities remain untaken.
It is not that his strength is insufficient to capture them.
The reason he has not attacked for three years
is that he wishes to prolong the display of military might to subdue the Qí people,
then face south and rule as king.
Now the Qí people are already subdued.
The reason he has not yet acted
is because his wife and children are in Yān.
Moreover, Qí has many beautiful women,
and he will soon forget his wife and children.
We hope Your Majesty will consider this!"
Zhāo Wáng then hosted a grand banquet,
summoned the speaker, and reprimanded him, saying:
*Ràng*
means 'to rebuke'.
"The former king (Yān Kuài) offered the entire state to the worthy as a matter of ritual,
not out of greed for land to pass down to his descendants.
It was due to the lack of virtue in the one to whom it was transmitted,
who could not bear the responsibility of the mandate,
leading to the people of the state not being submissive.
Qí was unprincipled,
taking advantage of the chaos in our lonely state to harm the former king."
This refers to Wáng Kuài yielding the state to Zǐ Zhī,
which led to the state's ruin and his own death.
The event is found in the previous volume under the fifth year of Shèn Jìng Wáng,
and this is the first year of the present king.
*Kān*
means 'to endure' or 'to be capable'.
'Could not bear the responsibility of the mandate'
means
Wáng Kuài mandated Zǐ Zhī,
but Zǐ Zhī could not bear what Wáng Kuài mandated nor manage the affairs of the Yān state.
*Kuài*
is pronounced *kǔ guài*.
*Jìng*
is pronounced *jí zhèng*.
*Shèng*
is pronounced *shēng*.
*Rèn*
is pronounced *rén*.
"The pain penetrated my bones,
so I widely sought out distinguished ministers
and invited guests from abroad,
to seek revenge.
If anyone achieved success,
I would even share the Yān state with them.
Now Lord Yuè has personally broken Qí for me,
flattening their ancestral temples."
*Yí*
means 'to flatten'.
*Wèi*
is pronounced *yú wěi*.
"The state of Qí rightfully belongs to Lord Yuè;
it is not something Yān has gained.
If Lord Yuè can possess Qí,
and stand alongside Yān as a co-equal state,
establishing friendly relations and a common bond
to resist the difficulties posed by other feudal lords,
that would be the good fortune of Yān
and my wish.
How dare you speak such words!"
He then executed the man.
He bestowed on Yuè Yì's wife the robes of a queen,
and on his son the robes of a ducal prince;
a royal chariot and a four-horse team,
followed by one hundred attendant chariots.
Xī Zhòng of Xià made chariots,
and their design was completed by the Zhōu dynasty.
The body was square, symbolizing the earth;
the canopy was round, symbolizing heaven;
thirty spokes symbolized the sun and moon;
twenty-eight canopy bows symbolized the constellations;
a dragon banner with nine streamers, seven *rèn* high, with a Qí-style linchpin, symbolized Dà Huǒ;
a bird banner with seven streamers, five *rèn* high, with a Qí-style chariot-front, symbolized Qún Huǒ;
a bear banner with six streamers,
five *rèn* high, with a Qí-style axle-end, symbolized Cān Fá;
a turtle banner with four streamers, four *rèn* high, with a Qí-style chariot-front, symbolized Yíng Shì;
a lone banner and a crooked arrow symbolized Hú: these were what feudal lords and lower ranks displayed.
After the royal chariot,
there were also one hundred attendant chariots,
which was also the custom of the various states at that time.
A four-horse team
means four horses.
Kǒng Yǐngdá said in *Shū Xù*: King Wǔ's war chariots numbered three hundred *liǎng*,
with each *chéng* counting as one *liǎng*.
They were called *liǎng* because,
according to *Fēngsú Tōng*, a chariot has two wheels,
hence chariots are referred to as *liǎng*.
*Chéng*
is pronounced *shéng zhèng*.
*Hǎo*
is pronounced *hū dào*.
*Nán*
is pronounced *nǎi dàn*.
*Shǔ*
is pronounced *shú*.
*Liǎng*
is pronounced *liàng*.
*Qí*
is pronounced *qú xī*.
*Yóu*
is pronounced *yí zhōu*,
meaning *liú*.
*Cān*
is pronounced *suǒ jīn*,
a star name of a constellation.
*Zhào*
is pronounced *zhào*.
He established Yuè Yì as King of Qí.
Yuè Yì, filled with apprehension, declined the offer,
bowing and writing a letter
vowing his loyalty unto death.
Because of this, the people of Qí admired his righteousness,
and the feudal lords feared his trustworthiness,
none daring to plot against him again.
A short while later,
Zhāo Wáng died,
and Huì Wáng ascended the throne.
*Qǐng zhī*
means 'after not much time'.
*Xiàng*
is pronounced *xī liàng*.
*Yì*
is pronounced *yú qì*.
(Huì Wáng) had long been displeased with Yuè Yì.
Tián Dān heard of this
and then sent a reverse spy into Yān.
Sūn Zǐ's five kinds of spies
include reverse spies,
which involve using enemy spies.
It also says: when enemy spies spy on us,
we then bribe them,
guide them, and let them go,
thus reverse spies can be used.
*Jiàn*
is pronounced *gǔ xiàn*.
"The King of Qí is already dead,
and only two cities remain untaken.
Yuè Yì has a rift with the new King of Yān,
fears execution, and dares not return.
He uses attacking Qí as a pretext,
but actually wishes to link his army with Qí and face south as King of Qí.
The people of Qí have not yet submitted,
so he is delaying his attack on Jìmò to await his opportunity.
What the Qí people fear
is only the arrival of another general,
for then Jìmò would be ruined."
The King of Yān already suspected Yuè Yì,
and upon receiving the Qí reverse spy's report,
he dispatched Qí Jié to replace him as general and recalled Yuè Yì.
Yuè Yì knew the King's intentions were not good.
'Replaced'
means knowing the King sent a replacement,
his intention was not good,
he intended to execute him.
The Yān generals and soldiers were thus resentful and disunited.
Tián Dān 令城中人食，
必祭其先祖於庭，
飛鳥皆翔舞而下城中。
燕人怪之，
Tián Dān 因宣言曰：
「當有神師下教我。」
有一卒曰：
「臣可以為師乎？」
因反走。
Tián Dān 起引還，
坐東鄉，
師事之。
卒曰：
「臣欺君。」
Tián Dān 曰：
「子勿言也！」
因師之。
每出約束，
必稱神師。
Tián Dān 恐衆心未一，
故假神以令其衆。
「吾唯懼燕軍之劓所得齊卒，
置之前行，
Jìmò 敗矣！」
燕人聞之，
如其言。
城中見降者盡劓，
皆怒，
堅守，
唯恐見得。
單又縱反間，
言
「吾懼燕人掘吾城外冢墓，
可為寒心！」
燕軍盡掘冢墓，
燒死人。
齊人從城上望見，
皆涕泣，
共欲出戰，
怒自十倍。
Tián Dān 知士卒之可用，
乃身操版、鍤，
與士卒分功；
妻妾編於行伍之間；
盡散飲食饗士。
令甲卒皆伏，
使老、弱、女子乘城，
乘，
登也，
登城而守也。
燕軍皆呼萬歲。
Tián Dān 又收民金得千鎰，
令 Jìmò 富豪遺燕將，
曰：
「即降，
願無虜掠吾族家！」
燕將大喜，
許之。
燕軍益懈。
Tián Dān 乃收城中，
得牛千餘，
為絳繒衣，
畫以五采龍文，
畫，
古[AS-FE61] [AS-FBEC] [AS-FD70] [AS-FBEC]一字通。
而灌脂束葦於其尾，
燒其端，
鑿城數十穴，
夜縱牛，
壯士五千
隨其後。
《史記·田單傳》，
「壯士五千」
下有
字。
怒而奔燕軍。
燕軍大驚，
視牛皆龍文，
所觸盡死傷。
而城中鼓譟從之，
老弱皆擊銅器為聲，
聲動天地。
燕軍大駭，
敗走。
齊人殺 Qí Jié，
追亡逐北，
亡，

北，

In the forty-ninth year, Wèi Qí fled to Zhào
and hid in Píngyuán Jūn's house.
Qín sent an envoy to tell the King of Zhào:
"If I do not get Qí's head,
I will not release your younger brother from the pass!"
Wèi Qí, in distress,
went to Yú Qīng.
Yú Qīng abandoned his prime minister's seal
and fled with Wèi Qí.
When they reached Wèi,
they wanted to use Xìnlíng Jūn to escape to Chǔ.
Xìnlíng Jūn hesitated to meet him.
Wèi Qí became angry
and committed suicide.
The King of Zhào eventually took his head and gave it to Qín,
and Qín then returned Píngyuán Jūn.
In the ninth month,
Wáng Líng, a Wǔdàfū, once again led troops
to attack Zhào.
Wǔ'ān Jūn was ill
and unfit to go.

Máo Suí recommended himself to Píngyuán-Jūn.

從 (cóng),

上 (shàng),

The city of Ānyǐng

鄢 (yān),

郢 (yǐng),

索 (suǒ),

Jìn,

desired to jointly honor Qín as Emperor.

is Fūrén Huáyáng.
Although Bùwéi is poor,
I request to use a thousand gold pieces to travel west for you,
and establish you as the heir."
Yìrén said:
"If it must be as you strategize,
I request to divide the state of Qín and share it with you."
Bùwéi then gave five hundred gold pieces to Yìrén,
instructing him to gather retainers.
He then used another five hundred gold pieces to buy rare objects and treasures,
and carrying them himself, went west.
He met Fūrén Huáyáng's elder sister,
and presented the rare objects to Fūrén.
He then praised the worthiness of Prince Yìrén,
saying that his retainers were all over the world,
and that he constantly wept day and night thinking of the Crown Prince and Fūrén,
saying:
"Yìrén truly regards Fūrén as his heaven!"
Fūrén was greatly pleased.
Bùwéi then had her elder sister persuade Fūrén, saying:
"One who serves others with her beauty,
when her beauty fades, her favor wanes.
Now Fūrén is favored but has no son.
If you do not, while in your prime, promptly ally yourself with a worthy and filial one among the princes,
and elevate him as heir,
then when your beauty fades and favor wanes,
even if you wish to utter a single word,
will it still be possible!
Now, Prince Yìrén is worthy,
and he himself knows that among the sons
he cannot be the heir.
If Fūrén indeed elevates him at this time,
then Prince Yìrén will have a state though he has none,
and Fūrén will have a son though she has none.
Then you will be favored by Qín for life."
Fūrén thought it was so,
and seizing an opportunity, spoke to the Crown Prince, saying:
"Prince Yìrén is exceptionally worthy."
Máo Huǎng said: "絕 (jué),
means 'exceptionally outstanding,'
'far apart' (from others in quality)."
She then wept and said:
"I am unfortunate to have no son.
I wish to adopt Prince Yìrén as my son
to entrust my person to him!"
The Crown Prince granted it,
and with Fūrén, carved a jade tally,
promising to make him heir.
They then generously gifted Yìrén,
and invited Lǚ Bùwéi to be his tutor.
Yìrén's reputation flourished among the feudal lords.
Lǚ Bùwéi married the most beautiful of the women in Hándān
and lived with her.
The character '娶' (qǔ)
should, according to the Shǐjì, be written as
Hándān,
pronounced Hándān.
Yìng Shào said: 娠 (shēn),
means 'tremble with pregnancy.'
The Zuǒzhuàn says: Yì Jiāng was just pregnant.
Mèng Kāng said: 娠 (shēn),
pronounced shēn,
in the Hànshū,
'娠' (shēn)
is often written as
'身' (shēn).
They are ancient and modern forms of the same character.
Shīgǔ said: Mèng's explanation is correct.
All instances in the Hànshū use 娠 (shēn) as the character for pregnancy.
Yì Jiāng was just shaking (with the first movements of pregnancy),
from the character for 'trembling' or 'shaking,'
not as 娠 (shēn).
Yìrén saw her and requested her.
Bùwéi feigned anger,
but soon presented her to him.
She was pregnant for a full year and gave birth to Zǐ Zhèng.
Yìrén then made her his Fūrén.
During the siege of Hándān,
the Zhào people wanted to kill him.
Yìrén and Bùwéi gave six hundred catties of gold to the guards,
escaped and fled to the Qín army,
and thus managed to return.
Yìrén, wearing Chǔ-style clothing, went to see Fūrén Huáyáng,
Chǔfú,
means the clothing of the Chǔ people.
Some say: 楚楚 (chǔchǔ),
means 'splendid attire.'
He said: "I am a man of Chǔ,
and should be adopted by you."
So he changed his name to Chǔ.
1 A Qín General, Liú, attacked Hán,
Liú,
Shǐjì Zhèngyì pronounces it "jǐ qiú fān".
Kāng said: It is pronounced "jū yóu qiè".
and decapitated forty thousand.
He attacked Zhào,
took more than twenty counties,
and decapitated or captured ninety thousand.
Nǎnwáng was afraid,
turned against Qín,
and allied with the feudal lords,
leading elite troops from all under heaven out of Yīquē to attack Qín.
He ordered that Yángchéng not be allowed passage.
The King of Qín sent General Liú to attack Xī Zhōu. Nǎnwáng entered Qín,
prostrated himself and accepted his guilt,
offering all thirty-six of his cities,
and thirty thousand inhabitants.
Qín accepted his offerings,
and returned Nǎnwáng to Zhōu.
In this year,
Nǎnwáng died.
Huángfǔ Mì said: The Zhōu had a total of thirty-seven kings,
for eight hundred and sixty-seven years.
